BRANCH IS STALE AND RED (found by the batch 6 merger, 2026-09-11). feat/standalone-invoice-create-page-merged adds a NEW call site at src/Controller/Admin/InvoiceController.php:863 calling applyLineQuantity() with the OLD four-argument shape. Main commit 2762cf23 (#659 step 3) widened AbstractAdminController::applyLineQuantity() to five parameters — (DenominatedLine $line, float $entered, float $baseQuantity, ?UnitOfMeasure $unit, ?UnitOfMeasure $base). Git merged the branch cleanly because the two changes are in different files, so this only appears at runtime: every standalone-invoice save path dies with ArgumentCountError. Nine of the ten Codeception failures in the seven-branch tree were this one cause. The merger called it an owner design call — 'what unit is a standalone invoice line denominated in' — and I initially passed that on. IT IS NOT OPEN: item 5 already ruled that product lines declare their unit and only blank lines keep free text, and a standalone invoice line is a product line. So the fix is to give the standalone create page the same unit selector the sales order line has and pass the real $unit and $base. Passing (null, null) would compile and go green, and it is the WRONG answer — applyLineQuantity() falls back to setQuantity() on a null unit, which would silently make the standalone invoice the one document in the app that ignores units. Do not take that shortcut.

items.title: Order line U/M: product lines should declare their unit; blank lines may keep free text
items.detail: The U/M cell renders a packaging_unit_id select when the product has rungs, else a free-text box. The fallback is wrong for PRODUCT lines — the product declares a base unit, so there is one correct answer and the box lets you type over it ('12P' seen live). It is RIGHT for BLANK lines, which describe something ad hoc with no product behind them and therefore nothing to declare a unit. The template already branches on type == 'product', so the distinction exists. Make product lines render the declared unit; leave blank lines free.
items.notes: LineDenomination::baseLabel() prefers the line's typed label over the product's declared base unit. That precedence is CORRECT for a blank line and wrong for a product line — applying it uniformly is the defect, not the precedence itself. Consequence is what a printed document SAYS, not what it computes: quantity_base comes from the packaging ladder, never from this label, so figures stay right while the stated unit can be wrong. line.baseUnitLabel is already computed for every line. Related to item 9 — the same unit-versus-pack-size conflation, but this one reaches a customer document.

items.title: Product import conflates unit of measure with pack size
items.detail: The import documents its unit column with the example '12/Case', which is a pack size, not a unit of measure. Under #601 those are product_packaging_unit rows. Products carrying such values declare no base unit and are flagged on the product form for a human.
items.notes:
Seen live: 'Anchor Bolt Sleeve M12 (bag of 50)' with U/M = BAG. If BAG is the base unit then stock is counted in bags, which changes what every quantity on that product means.

Built as ACCEPT-AND-FLAG, not reject. A row whose unit column holds a pack size ('12/Case', 'bag of 50', 'BAG') imports in full, leaves product_core.unit_id NULL, keeps the file's own words as the label a person resolves from, and is counted as flagged on the run page; the product form then opens on 'Not set' and names the pack size as what needs settling. No import of any shape creates a unit_of_measure row. Six conducted cases (#624), each carrying a row that must NOT move, plus a positive control proving 'EA' and 'Box' still resolve by code and by name. ONE THING IS STILL OPEN and is on the decision sheet: a flagged product is usable while its unit is unresolved. Whether it should be blocked until someone settles it is the owner's call.

OWNER RULING (2026-09-12) on the half left open: a product whose unit could not be resolved imports as a DRAFT, and is then QUEUED FOR ESCALATION so somebody fixes it. Owner: "Draft? Then queued for escalation to fix?" This is better than the blocking I proposed, for two reasons. It says WHY the product cannot be used, in vocabulary the app already speaks, instead of being an inert flag; and it makes the backlog a real work list rather than a property nobody looks at. It also needs no new column — ProductCore::$status already exists (src/Entity/ProductCore.php:77, a plain string defaulting to 'Active', no enum), so Draft is a value in a field that is already there.

WHAT THE THREE REFERENCE PRODUCTS DO, looked up rather than assumed: none of them has a flagged-but-usable state, because the unit is mandatory at creation. Zoho Inventory makes Unit a required field and its import SKIPS rows missing it into a skipped-records file you fix and re-import. Business Central makes Base Unit of Measure mandatory and — the decisive part — you CANNOT CHANGE IT once a ledger entry has posted against the item; the workaround for a wrong base unit is to block the item and create a new one. NetSuite: no clean source found, not asserted.

WHY THAT MATTERS HERE, and it is the whole argument for not leaving a flagged product transactable: if stock moves at an unknown unit, that is exactly the state in which the unit can no longer be safely corrected. Letting it transact converts a pending problem into a permanent one. Draft prevents that while keeping the row visible and editable.

BUILD NOTES. The escalation queue should follow the count-tile rule already recorded: it renders only when it has something to report, so a clean instance shows nothing. 'Be clear and be loud' applies at the point of import too — the run page already reports how many rows were flagged; it should say they are Drafts and link straight to them. And check what currently reads ProductCore::$status before adding a value to it: a free-string status with no enum means the set of legal values lives in whatever queries and templates test it, so find them all rather than assuming 'Active' is the only one anybody checks for.

items.detail: unit_of_measure grows the ratio column for every family including quantity (Box-12 and Box-24 are separate terms). New join table: which units a product may use. items.title: Break a case / unbreak a case: two SKUs, one stock transaction
items.detail: Distributors buy packaged goods where the case and the unit are DIFFERENT SKUs — two product rows, two inventory balances. Warehouse staff break a case into units, and sometimes rebuild one. Today there is nowhere to enter that: it can only be done as two unrelated manual adjustments, which leaves no record that one caused the other. Needs (a) a declared relationship between the two SKUs saying one case SKU holds N of the unit SKU, and (b) a screen that takes 'break 3 cases of SKU-CASE' and writes both sides at once.
items.notes:
NOT units of measure, and the distinction is the whole point (#659). A unit of measure converts a quantity WITHIN one SKU — 40 Case of SKU-X is 480 eaches of SKU-X, one inventory balance, no transaction. Two SKUs are two balances, and moving stock between them is a real event that must be recorded, dated and attributable, exactly like a transfer. NetSuite treats this the same way: same item, use a unit; different items, use an assembly build/unbuild. Merging the two would let a unit conversion silently move stock between products. Likely home: modules/InventoryDepthBundle. InventoryMovementGroup already exists for precisely this shape — 'one operation: the reason, the actor, the reference, and the movements it caused' — and already enumerates receipt/putaway/pick/ship/transfer/move/status_change/adjustment/vendor_return, so this is a new group type writing two movements (out of the case SKU, into the unit SKU) under one group, not a new ledger. Nothing today implements assembly, kits or a bill of materials, so there is no existing concept to extend.

Built as a real dated stock transaction between two SKUs, not a unit conversion — the distinction #659 turns on. Carries migration Version20260912064215, ADD-only. Its new screen is proven to disappear when the bundle is switched off (a 404, asserted), though see item 52: the gate that was supposed to prove that had never run.

items.title: The same goods can be billed twice, on two different vendor bills, and nothing objects
items.detail: Nothing compares a bill line against what other bills have already charged for the same purchase order line. Sequence: 100 units arrive against PO line X. Enter bill A for 100 against X, approve it — the three-way match reports clean. The vendor sends a second invoice under a different number; enter bill B, also against the same PO, also for 100 against X, approve it — the match reports clean again. Each bill line is only ever compared against the PO line's TOTAL received quantity, never against the quantity already billed by other bills, so the second bill looks exactly as correct as the first. The business has now approved payment for 200 units it received 100 of, and no exception was raised on either document. The received-but-not-billed report hides the evidence instead of showing it: it skips any line whose billed quantity has reached its received quantity, so an over-billed line silently disappears from the accrual list rather than showing a negative. The one duplicate guard that exists matches on the vendor's own invoice NUMBER, so it catches the same PDF keyed in twice but never two genuinely different invoices covering the same delivery.
items.notes: MONEY DEFECT — this is the one that lets real cash leave for goods never received, and it needs no mistake beyond entering a second invoice. Cause: modules/ProcurementBundle/src/Controller/Admin/VendorBillController.php:207 attaches a bill line to a PO line (setPurchaseOrderLine) inside the save loop at :185 with no check of any kind against existing bills; the save route is :128. The match does not catch it either — modules/ProcurementBundle/src/Match/ThreeWayMatchService.php:172 tests this bill line's quantity (:143) against the PO line's total received (:166), a comparison with no term for what other bills hold. Approval never blocks regardless: VendorBillController.php:241 records exceptions on the timeline and proceeds. THE FIX MATERIAL ALREADY EXISTS: ExceptionController.php:181 billedQuantityFor() already sums billed quantity per PO line across all live bills and already excludes Draft and Void, which is exactly the figure a guard needs; it is called only at ExceptionController.php:153, for the accrual list, and ExceptionController.php:156 is the skip that hides the over-billing. Note for whoever picks this up: the billed-quantity link is the PURCHASE ORDER line, not the goods-receipt line — VendorBillLine has purchaseOrderLine and no receipt-line association at all — so a guard belongs on the PO line's running total. The existing number-only warning is ThreeWayMatchService.php:126, deliberately warn-never-block; a quantity guard is a different question and should not be folded into it.

items.title: Five vendor-return and debit-memo links are stored but never filled in
items.detail: Five columns exist in the database, are mapped on the entities, have working setters, and are never written by anything — no screen, no controller, no command, no seed. The consequences a person meets: you cannot tell which vendor bill a debit memo was raised from, nor which bill line a memo line disputes, so a memo arrives at the vendor with no stated provenance and nobody can answer 'what is this against?' later. You cannot tell which purchase order a vendor return belongs to, so returns do not show against the order that bought the goods. You cannot tell which delivery a returned line came off, even though the return screen was built FROM a goods receipt and had that row in its hand while drawing the form. And a refund on a debit memo records no person, so there is no answer to who paid it out — the sales side records exactly that on its own refunds.
items.notes:
DATA-INTEGRITY DEFECT: each of these is provenance that can never be reconstructed after the fact, so every day the columns stay unwritten is history that cannot be backfilled. Confirmed one by one — setter exists, zero call sites outside the entity's own file, across the whole repository including modules/ProcurementBundle/src/Command/SeedProcurementDemoDataCommand.php. (1) vendor_return.purchase_order_id — VendorReturn::setPurchaseOrder at modules/ProcurementBundle/src/Entity/VendorReturn.php:136; the save that should call it sets only vendor, goodsReceipt, reason and notes at VendorReturnController.php:132-136. (2) vendor_return_line.goods_receipt_line_id — VendorReturnLine::setGoodsReceiptLine at modules/ProcurementBundle/src/Entity/VendorReturnLine.php:72; the line build at VendorReturnController.php:156-162 omits it, and the evidence that the data was right there is templates/vendor_return_edit.html.twig:33-34, which loops over receipt.lines and emits product_id, name, sku and quantity per row but no hidden id for the receipt line itself. (3) debit_memo.vendor_bill_id — DebitMemo::setVendorBill at modules/ProcurementBundle/src/Entity/DebitMemo.php:109; DebitMemo.php:19 documents it as PROVENANCE ('raised from BILL-123'); the save at DebitMemoController.php:120-126 sets vendorReturn but never vendorBill, and the form has no field for it. (4) debit_memo_line.vendor_bill_line_id — DebitMemoLine::setVendorBillLine at modules/ProcurementBundle/src/Entity/DebitMemoLine.php:69, zero call sites anywhere. (5) debit_memo_refund.user_id — DebitMemoRefund::setUser at modules/ProcurementBundle/src/Entity/DebitMemoRefund.php:65; the refund build at DebitMemoController.php:258-261 omits it, while the sales-side equivalent does record it at src/Controller/Admin/CreditMemoController.php:426 — direct proof of the intended pattern and that the procurement mirror simply dropped this line. All five columns are migrated and real: migrations/Version20260908180000.php:102 (vendor_return), :110 (vendor_return_line), :114 (debit_memo), :119 (debit_memo_line), :126 (debit_memo_refund). Note the near-misses that are NOT defects and should not be swept up with these: debit_memo.vendor_return_id IS written (DebitMemoController.php:125), vendor_return.goods_receipt_id IS written (VendorReturnController.php:135), and vendor_return.warehouse_id IS written, as a parameter to VendorReturn::ship() rather than by a setter. CORRECTION x2, both from the agent that wired them. (1) 'zero call sites across the whole repo including the seed command' was WRONG for two of the five: SeedProcurementVolumeCommand writes vendor_return_line.goods_receipt_line_id (:986, read back :1167) and debit_memo.vendor_bill_id (:1159, read :1211). The accurate statement is zero APPLICATION call sites for all five; the volume seeder writes two. The original note named only SeedProcurementDemoDataCommand, which indeed writes none. (2) There is a SIXTH: debit_memo_line.product_id was written by nothing either — not the controller, not the volume seeder — and it is what lets a restock memo say WHAT went back. All six are now wired rather than dropped, because each has a sell-side twin that is written, so they were dropped lines rather than unwanted columns.

The dead provenance links are written. items.title: A vendor return raised by mistake can only be got rid of by claiming the vendor authorised it
items.detail: A vendor return starts life as Requested. Its lines can still be edited at that point, but there is no way to cancel, delete or decline it. Decline is refused unless the return is already Authorised or Shipped, Close is refused unless it is Shipped, and no delete route exists. The detail screen agrees with the state machine: on a Requested return the only button offered is Authorise. So a return raised against the wrong vendor, or entered twice, can only be cleared by first clicking Authorise — which stamps an authorised-at date and asserts the vendor agreed to take the goods back, something that never happened — and then immediately Declining it. The document is left permanently recording a vendor agreement that was invented purely to close it. It is worse for a return raised with no lines on it, or whose lines are all zero: Authorise refuses those outright for having nothing on them, so the document cannot be authorised, declined, closed or deleted, and sits on the vendor returns list forever with no exit at all.
items.notes: Affects VENDOR RETURNS ONLY — debit memos were checked and are fine, so this must not be written up as a shared defect. A draft debit memo is editable (DebitMemoController.php:106 guards on isDraft) and can be killed directly: DebitMemo::void() at modules/ProcurementBundle/src/Entity/DebitMemo.php:175 refuses only when the memo is already void or has something applied or refunded against it, so a draft with nothing on it voids cleanly. Vendor returns are the ones with no escape. Evidence: modules/ProcurementBundle/src/Entity/VendorReturn.php:205 decline() requires Authorised or Shipped; :225 close() requires Shipped; :156 authorise() is the only move out of Requested and :163 refuses a return with no units on it. The controller exposes only authorise, decline and close — VendorReturnController.php:186 — with no delete or cancel route anywhere in the bundle. The screen matches: templates/vendor_return_detail.html.twig:41-45 shows Authorise alone while Requested, and :71 gates Decline on Authorised or Shipped. Line editing while Requested does work (VendorReturnController.php:119 via VendorReturnStatus::allowsLineEditing() at src/Enum/VendorReturnStatus.php:42), so the gap is specifically a missing cancel, not a missing edit. Likely shape of the fix, for whoever takes it: allow decline() from Requested as well, or add a Cancel that is honest about the document never having left the building — a decision about what the vendor agreed to, so worth confirming with the owner before building. IN PROGRESS 2026-09-11: branch fix/vendor-return-cannot-be-cancelled, commit ce7b41b9, pushed. decline() now refuses only isTerminal(), the idiom Rfq::cancel() and RfqVendorReply::decline() already use, so Requested -> Declined is allowed and Declined stays the single abandon verb rather than adding a second terminal not-happening state. Everything that should still be forbidden is asserted to still be forbidden: ship() demands Authorised, close() demands Shipped, lines freeze past Requested, Closed and Declined are terminal, and authorise() still refuses an empty return. Measured: 3 conducted tests, 175 assertions, pass on the fix and ALL THREE FAIL on the original code. Worse, `12abc` is cast to customer 12 and shown with no warning at all. Same shape on the credit memo and sales return lists. items.title: The SELL side can double-invoice the same order line, through drafts
items.detail: Invoice::countsTowardInvoicedQuantity() excludes Draft. So two draft invoices can each claim a sales order line in full — neither sees the other, because neither counts — and both can then be issued. The customer is invoiced twice for one delivery.
items.blocked_by: src/Entity/Invoice.php is core. Needs a core-scoped change.
items.notes:
The exact twin of the purchase-side defect fixed on feat/bill-parity-and-billing-guards, found while fixing it. The buy side's answer is already written and proven, and it is two methods rather than one: claimsOrderedQuantity() (not Void — drafts INCLUDED) backs the guard that refuses over-billing at save, because two drafts each claiming the whole line is the case that actually happens; counts() (not Draft, not Void — drafts EXCLUDED) backs accrual and aging, because a draft has authorised nothing and the goods should stay reported unbilled while somebody is mid-typing. Both live on VendorBillStatus with each docblock naming the other and the single case they disagree on. The sell side needs the same split — today it has only the accrual reading, and uses it for both jobs, which is why the hole exists. A money defect: unlike the purchase side there is no exceptions screen to even surface it after the fact.

DONE. AND THIS ITEM'S OWN DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, corrected by the agent that landed it. The note above says the sell side 'has only the accrual reading, and uses it for both jobs, which is why the hole exists'. That is not the mechanism. The sell side used the accrual reading for ONE job — derivation — and had NO claim check after raise at all: OrderInvoicingService checked when an invoice was raised and nothing ever looked again. Adding a second predicate without moving the gate would have closed nothing.

The fix is GATE PLACEMENT, not predicate count. The guard moved to Invoice::issue()/issueAwaitingPayment(), the moment a sell-side invoice actually takes quantity off the line, and is unreachable around it — transitionTo() is private and there is no setStatus() anywhere in src/. Drafts therefore need not claim, which is why the sell side needs only countsTowardInvoicedQuantity() where the buy side needs both: the buy side guards at SAVE and approval has no guard, so if its drafts did not claim, two drafts would both save and both approve. A sell-side claimsOrderedQuantity() would have no consumer — there is no sell-side accrual or aging report.

The cost is stated rather than hidden: on the buy side you learn at save with the figures in front of you; here you type the whole invoice and are refused at Issue. That is the owner's ruling that two drafts may coexist, made concrete. If that ruling is ever reversed into a save-time guard, THEN the sell side needs the second predicate.

items.title: A draft document should be deletable
items.detail: No document type in this app can be deleted — not orders, invoices, estimates, credit memos, sales returns, purchase orders, bills, RFQs, vendor returns or debit memos. Only child records (payments, refunds, log entries) have delete routes. So a draft raised by mistake can only be abandoned into a terminal state, and the list fills with declined typos nobody can tell from real history.
items.notes: Owner's ruling: a draft is safe to delete. I raised two supposed hazards and ONE OF THEM WAS WRONG — correcting it here so nobody designs around a danger that does not exist. (1) WRONG: I said a draft SALES ORDER may hold a backorder reservation. It does not. SalesOrderBackorderReservationSubject and BackorderQueueSynchronizer both gate on OrderInventoryBucketResolver::bucketForStatus(), and both say so in their own comments — 'a Draft reserves nothing' and 'a Draft has promised nothing yet'. I flagged it as unconfirmed and should have confirmed it before raising it. (2) REAL, and being fixed: a draft INVOICE can carry payments. There is no status check in InvoiceController::savePayment(), in payments(), or in the template, so a Draft accepts payments and — because payment status is derived from the rows by InvoicePaymentStatusSubscriber at flush — can display itself as Paid while still a draft nobody has seen. Fixed on fix/sell-side-double-invoicing: the screen is not offered on a draft and the POST is refused server-side, because hiding a control is not a guard in an app that works with scripting off. Once that lands, 'draft is safe to delete' holds with no carve-outs. The number should still be BURNT rather than reused: a gap in a document sequence cannot be told apart from a lost record, which is the reason no ERP deletes a numbered document. This remains a whole-app convention change rather than a per-document one.

items.title: A payment cannot be moved from one invoice to another
items.detail: A payment recorded against the wrong invoice can only be deleted and re-keyed. There is no route to move it: admin_invoice_payments records, admin_invoice_payment_delete removes, and nothing reassigns. Deleting and re-entering loses the original received date, method, reference and who recorded it, unless whoever does it copies all of that by hand first.
items.notes:
Surfaced by the owner's ruling that an invoice holding payments cannot be cancelled — the remedies are to remove the payment or move it, and only the first exists. So the refusal message currently has to offer half an answer. Zoho Books, which the owner named as the reference for the cancellation rule, does let a payment be reassigned. Worth doing properly rather than as a delete-and-recreate shortcut: the payment row carries its own identity and history, and a move should preserve it, adjusting the derived payment status on BOTH invoices — the one losing the payment may cease to be Paid, and the one gaining it may become Paid. InvoicePaymentStatusSubscriber derives that at flush from the rows, so a move must make both documents recalculate, not just the destination.

OWNER RULING (2026-09-12): BUILD IT NOW. "it's just an extra dropdown hand it out to a worker damnit. Same for purchase payments too." So the scope is BOTH SIDES — moving an invoice payment between invoices, and moving a vendor bill payment between bills (VendorBillPayment). From the user's side it is a dropdown on the payment; the work behind it is that the payment row keeps its own identity and history rather than being deleted and recreated, and that the derived paid status is recalculated on BOTH documents — the one losing the payment may cease to be Paid, the one gaining it may become Paid.

EXTENDED BY THE OWNER: "Payments in both sides should share a shape through our common strategy." So this is not two lookalike implementations — it is one declared payment contract with a discovering conformance test, built the way CommercialDocument already is. See _decisions.

items.title: A sidebar item can render as an icon affordance on another row
items.detail: Every create screen currently occupies a whole sidebar row of its own — New PO, New Bill, New Goods Receipt, Create Credit Note, Create Order. Zoho puts a + on the right of the list item instead, revealed on hover, so New Retainer Invoice is one click from Retainer Invoices rather than a second row. Add an opt-in flag so an existing create item renders as a + on a named parent row. Generalised on the owner's suggestion: the flag also names WHICH icon, so the row-affordance slot is not hardcoded to create. A plus today; a search, a cog, an export later.
items.notes:
The owner's design, and it is better than mine. I proposed giving the PARENT an optional create route; the owner's version flags the EXISTING create item instead, so it keeps its own route, label, permission and identity and only its rendering changes — nothing new is declared and removing the flag puts the row back. One refinement agreed: the item NAMES its parent (attachTo: 'purchases.orders') rather than attaching to whatever is above it. Position is fragile here — ordering is numeric, bundles inject into the same groups, and App Management can reorder — so 'the one above me' would silently attach to the wrong row with nothing erroring. Naming it also gives a real error when the target is missing. Opt-in, so unflagged items render exactly as today: no migration, no big-bang, and the sidebar snapshot fixture only changes for items actually flagged. Also settled: reveal on `:hover, :focus-within` (pure CSS, no JS — the focus half is what stops a keyboard user tabbing to something invisible); use opacity/visibility rather than display:none, which would take it out of the tab order and the accessibility tree; always-visible below a touch breakpoint, since touch devices have no hover at all; and the accessible name must be the item's own label ('New Bill'), never '+', or a screen reader reads out a row of plus signs. Whether the create ROW then goes away is a separate, per-item decision the flag makes trivially reversible — keep both first, delete later if the row stops earning its place. Note create routes are NOT consistently named (admin_bundle_procurement_bill_new beside admin_bundle_procurement_vendor_create), so nothing here can be derived by convention; that is another reason to flag the existing item rather than have a parent guess its create route. GENERALISED (owner): the flag carries the ICON as well as the parent — attachTo plus icon: 'plus' — so this is a row-affordance slot rather than a create-button feature, and a second kind of affordance later needs no further design. Two consequences to settle when building. (1) ORDER AND LIMIT: two icons on a sidebar row is already tight and three is cramped. Decide whether affordances sort by the item's existing order number, and either cap them or write down plainly that nobody should assume room for five. (2) ACCESSIBLE NAMES come free from this design and would NOT from mine: every affordance is still a real menu item with its own label, route and permission, so each icon already has something true to announce. An icon invented on the parent row would have had no name, no route and no permission of its own — which is the strongest argument for the owner's version over the one I proposed. ACCESSIBLE NAME FIELD (owner): add an explicit, OPTIONAL accessible-name field on the item, falling back to the item's own label when absent — additive, so nothing existing needs it and no item has to be touched. Worth having even though the label is usually right, because it is not always right IN CONTEXT: a cog labelled 'Settings' sitting on a row called 'Purchases' should announce 'Purchase Settings', since 'Settings' alone reads as a generic link wherever a screen reader encounters it. The fallback keeps the common case free while letting the odd case be stated. Same additive shape as the rest of this item: opt-in flag, opt-in icon, opt-in name, nothing removed, no migration, and the sidebar snapshot fixture changes only for items actually flagged. BUILT on feat/sidebar-row-affordances @ fb2f8780 (not merged). Eight create items exist in the sidebar and all eight are flagged: Add Product, Add Company, Create Quote, Create Order, Create Credit Note, New PO, New Bill, New Goods Receipt. accessibleName used on three of eight, which is the right proportion for an optional field — an abbreviation (New PO), a screen name in the wrong order (Product Add), and a genuinely ambiguous one (Create Order, in a sidebar that also has Purchase Orders). Deliberately NOT flagged, each argued: derived screens that cannot be created (Exceptions, AP Aging, Low Stock, Discrepancies, Movements, Expected Arrivals, Backorders), hubs, lists and consoles, every settings screen, Product Import (a process, not a document), and inventory.adjust (an operation with no adjustments list to sit on). OPEN QUESTION FOR THE OWNER, do not decide it unattended: five create routes have NO sidebar item to flag — RFQ, debit memo, vendor return, vendor price and vendor create, all reached from their list screens instead. Same for sales return, customer user, warehouse and two warehouse-ops creates. Giving them a + means ADDING new sidebar rows, because the flag is additive and a new item brings a row with it. That is a visible change to the Vendors and Purchases groups that nobody asked for, and it is not what the owner authorised when they said 'we're literally reordering and adding 2 attributes'. Five SCREENS entries, one line each, if they want it. Two judgement calls worth keeping: a HIDDEN target is deliberately not logged, because that is an admin configuring their own sidebar and warning about it would train people to ignore warnings; and the bare-button degrade sets an explicit 22x22 hit area with a focus-visible outline, because an empty anchor collapses to zero width and a colour swap on an empty box is not a focus indicator anyone can see.

Built to the owner's design: the EXISTING create item names its parent and only its rendering changes, so it keeps its own route, label, permission and identity, and removing the flag puts the row back. A missing icon degrades to a plain button rather than breaking the menu. STILL OPEN and on the decision sheet: five create routes have no sidebar item at all, so giving them a '+' means ADDING five rows rather than flagging existing ones.

items.title: The inventory screen shows 7 of 14 buckets, and Available cannot be reconciled from it
items.detail: product_inventory carries 14 quantity fields; templates/admin/inventory/_rows.html.twig renders 7 — Starting, Received, Hold, Sales Hold, Pending, Approved, Backordered — plus Available and the backorder cap. Invisible: reserved, incoming (on order from vendors), quarantine (received but not accepted), transfer in, transfer out, and write-off. Owner also asks for a warehouse chooser, and for the stacked backorder cell (Allow backorder / Max / Shrink cap on restock / Auto-release on restock, four controls in one cell) to become proper columns.
items.notes:
The defect is not 'columns are missing', it is that AVAILABLE CANNOT BE RECONCILED. On the owner's own screenshot the arithmetic works — 100 - 4 - 4 = 92, 180 - 30 = 150 — but only because every hidden bucket happens to be zero. The moment one is not, the page shows a figure that does not add up from anything visible and offers nothing to click to find out why. Likely history is the familiar one: the screen was built for the core buckets, then procurement added incoming, receiving added quarantine and warehouse ops added transfers, and nobody returned to the screen. OWNER ALSO ASKS FOR A GUARD, and it is the valuable half: a conformance test asserting that every quantity bucket on the entity appears on this table, discovered from Doctrine metadata rather than a hand-kept list, so a bundle adding a bucket cannot silently fail to show it. The app already has this habit twice — ProductBaseUnitService::quantityColumns() sweeps the mapping, and AdminListScreenConventionsCest discovers its subjects from the router — so follow that shape, including a named-exception list whose entries are asserted to STILL be excluded. One tension to resolve rather than ignore: six more buckets plus four backorder columns makes a very wide table. The warehouse chooser helps, but choosing COLUMNS would help more, since most people want Available and two or three buckets rather than all fourteen.

All 14 buckets, a warehouse filter and a column chooser, with a conformance test that a newly added bucket must appear on the screen. ProductInventory::reservedQuantity was verified to be permanently 0 with no writer and absent from getAvailableQuantity(), and was deliberately left alone — it is shown marked 'not counted' rather than quietly dropped.

items.title: Voiding a credit memo leaves the customer's returned stock on your books
items.detail: The sell-side twin of the debit memo defect. A credit memo that restocked a customer return can be voided, and the stock movement is not reversed — so inventory stays UP with no live document behind it. CreditMemo::void() has no guard against it.
items.blocked_by: src/Entity/CreditMemo.php is core. The owner has approved this change specifically.
items.notes: Owner's ruling: same treatment as the buy side. Voiding offers THREE outcomes, each stating its real effect in concrete terms — the product, the quantity, the warehouse, the direction, and which bucket it lands in — because 'an adjustment will be created' is not something a person can consent to. (1) BACK IN STOCK: a real movement, inventory returns to sellable. (2) WRITTEN OFF: a real movement into the write-off bucket, NOT into available stock — the owner says this is typically what a void means, 'something's wrong, the shit's bad, u have to write it off'. Check what already writes product_inventory.writeOffQuantity and use it rather than inventing a parallel path; if nothing writes it, that is its own finding. (3) GONE: a ZERO-QUANTITY movement. Nothing moves; the row exists to say so. The owner chose a zero row over a note deliberately — the ledger is the chronological record of everything, and if 'gone' were the only outcome with no entry then the one case where nothing happened would be the one case with no trace, which is exactly the case someone will later be trying to explain. My objection that zero rows force filtering was wrong: a zero adds nothing to SUM(quantity). The real costs are narrower — a COUNT of movements includes it, and anything treating 'has movements' as 'stock moved' reads wrong — and both are handled by the group type saying what it is. Cancel does nothing at all. All three go under their own InventoryMovementGroup carrying reason, actor and reference, all three appear on the timeline, and the memo's own detail screen shows what became of the goods so nobody has to go find the product to learn it. Direction differs from the buy side and is easy to invert: a sell-side restock brings goods IN, so inventory went UP and the reversal takes it DOWN. Mirror whatever lands on fix/debit-memo-and-vendor-return-gaps rather than designing it again. THE BUY SIDE IS BUILT on fix/debit-memo-and-vendor-return-gaps @ e8589895 — mirror it rather than designing again. Three implementation facts that cost that agent real work to establish. (1) DO NOT use AutomaticSourcePicker for the reversal: it only ever reads `available` rows, so it cannot source stock that is already written off. The buy side uses ReversalPlanner, this app's existing put-that-write-off-back path, which buys two things a hand-built pair of DetailKeys would not — both sides come off the ORIGINAL rows, so units land back in the exact bin, lot and serial they left, and its bound of `original.quantity - SUM(already reversed)` makes putting the same units back twice impossible. (2) WRITTEN OFF is a status move between two write-off statuses, NOT put-it-back-then-write-it-off — so `available` never rises and the write-off bucket does not jump; the units simply stop being described as sitting with the counterparty. (3) NO NEW COLUMN and no flag: 'did this memo move stock' is read from the LEDGER via the restock group's client_operation_id, which is where the fact is actually true, so it cannot drift — and it is right for free in the case a flag would have had to special-case, a memo whose products are all on simple inventory, which wrote no group and so voids with no question asked. Also settled by that work: product_inventory.write_off_quantity is NOT an unwritten bucket — the adjustment screen's damaged/spoiled/scrapped/lost reasons and vendor returns both write it. And no stored InventoryAdjustmentReason is attached to these groups, because each such row declares its own (from_status, to_status) pair and borrowing one would make the row assert something untrue; the classification lives in the group's reason text.

items.title: Four admin lists fetch every row, unpaged, into a bare table
items.detail: /admin/redirect, /admin/bundles/news, /admin/bundles/fees/user-defined and /admin/bundles/payments/manual each load every row in the table and render them with no pagination and no filters — the same shape the backorders screen had. Fine at twenty rows, a page that never finishes loading at twenty thousand.
items.notes: Found by the conformance rule that closed the PLAIN loophole, not by anyone looking. Each is currently an argued PLAIN_LISTS entry, asserted to STILL be plain — so conforming one fails the test until its entry goes, and none can rot silently. The fix is the one already proven twice: adopt `.content-frame > .table-card`, which is simultaneously the filter fix and the width fix, because the full-height clamp at app.css:7764 is a rule on that selector. Judge each on whether filters earn their place rather than adding them to satisfy a rule — a redirect table or a handful of manual payment methods may legitimately need none, in which case the shape alone is the fix. Four OTHER screens the same sweep flagged are NOT defects and are argued as such: the receiving scan tally (its state lives in the URL, not a table — the one case the empty-state signal genuinely cannot distinguish), the receiving-rules table inside the procurement settings form, the bin map, and the pick-list compile form's candidate set. Three of those four are warehouse, which the owner has parked.

items.title: A bill needs a payable figure separate from its balance arithmetic
items.detail: VendorBill::getBalance() is amount minus payments, and that is CORRECT as arithmetic — a voided bill with no payments genuinely has a balance of its full amount, and Zoho shows it the same way. What is missing is a second figure: what is actually PAYABLE, which is zero when the bill is void or draft. Today that rule lives only in AP Aging's query and the 'still owed' filter, so anyone writing a new report and summing getBalance() across bills gets a wrong AP total with nothing stopping them.
items.notes: ORIGINALLY FILED WRONG by me, and the owner corrected it twice. The sweep reported a voided bill showing 'Balance CAD 856.00' as a money defect. It is not: balance due is amount minus payments, full stop, and both a voided and a draft bill legitimately show their full amount because no payments were made against them. The owner checked Zoho and it behaves identically. So the fix is NOT to zero getBalance() or to hide it. TWO THINGS ARE ACTUALLY WANTED. (1) A separate method for the real AP figure — zero when void or draft, the balance otherwise — so the rule lives on the document rather than being re-derived correctly in AP Aging and forgotten by the next report. The owner's framing: a void bill 'is not applicable from the perspective of AP'. (2) The remaining display defect collapses entirely into item 41 — the page shows a large balance and never says the bill is void, because one core CSS rule hides the status on every purchase document. Fix 41 and there is nothing left to fix here beyond the method. Correct table shape, per the owner: Amount = the document's own figure, Balance due = amount minus payments, Status = Void/Draft shown. AP report = nothing.

items.title: One CSS rule hides the status on every purchase document
items.detail: A purchase order never shows its own status. 'Cancelled' appears nowhere on a cancelled PO, 'Closed' nowhere on a closed one, 'Disputed' nowhere on a disputed bill. The templates DO write it — purchase_order_detail.html.twig:7 passes 'vendor -> warehouse · status' as the page lead — but public/assets/css/app.css:611-615 hides every .lead and .eyebrow inside a .panel-title-row with display:none !important. The same rule swallows the document date, the expected date and the units outstanding.
items.notes: OWNER RULING (2026-09-11): "dont hide status. status should be in tables and on the detail page, big and loud". So the fix is the core CSS rule, not 31 bundle templates: delete/narrow public/assets/css/app.css:611-615 so .lead and .eyebrow render inside .panel-title-row. Status is additionally promoted to its own prominent badge on every document detail page and to a column on every document list, buy side and sell side alike. This also settles the DISPLAY half of item 40 (a void bill must read Void on screen); item 40 keeps only the separate-payable-figure work. Consequence still to price in: a CLOSED purchase order still offers 'Send to vendor' and the controller refuses only Draft and Cancelled.

items.title: You cannot see which purchase orders are late
items.detail: Expected Arrivals sorts by date and today shows 2026-01-15, 2026-06-07, 2026-06-12 at the top — up to eight months overdue, in the same plain black as next week's. No overdue badge, no count, no filter. The word 'overdue' does not occur anywhere in the bundle outside AP Aging's own hidden subtitle. The single date box means 'due on or before' and ALWAYS also returns orders with no expected date, so you cannot even approximate it by typing today.
items.notes:
Chasing late deliveries is the core daily task of a buyer, and the app cannot answer it. From the usability sweep. The date filter also quietly widening to include null expected dates is its own small defect — a filter that returns rows outside what you asked for.

OWNER RULING (2026-09-12), and it is GENERAL, not specific to this item: "Colouring is fine but should use shared class names and core css defines all classes that we know of. So all objects with similar traits eg 'late' is same treatment." So a screen never invents its own colour or its own class. Core CSS owns the vocabulary, every class it knows of is defined there, and a trait means the same thing everywhere it appears — 'late' looks identical on a purchase order, an invoice, a sales order and a backorder, because it IS the same trait. A bundle that needs a trait core does not yet name asks for it to be added to core rather than styling locally.

So item 42 is APPROVED as planned — a red Overdue badge, a count, an Overdue-only filter, and the date box fixed to stop also returning purchase orders with no expected date — with the constraint that the badge uses a shared core `late` trait class, not a procurement-local one. STILL UNANSWERED: whether the procurement landing page should carry an 'Overdue: 12' tile. That question overlaps item 48 and should be settled there rather than asked twice.

items.title: The vendor page answers nothing about the vendor
items.detail: Not one link on a vendor's page reaches a document raised against them — every link edits the vendor record itself. No orders, no bills, no balance, no receipts, no returns, no spend. Answering 'what do we owe Steelhead and what is on order' means leaving and filtering four separate lists.
items.notes:
Made worse by AP Aging: the vendor name in each aging row IS a link, and it lands here — so the drill-down from 'Blackrock owes CAD 1142.22, over 90 days' arrives at a contact-card editor. The company record gained document subtabs today (item 2, merged); this is the same job on the buy side and should mirror it. The sweep also found the vendor page is the ONLY purchasing screen showing database names to a person — nine on screen including payment_term_id, purchase_order.vendor_id and vendor_address.province — and that it carries two Notes sections, one labelled 'Notes (legacy field)'.

OWNER RULING (2026-09-12): mirror the customer page — subtabs POs, Bills, Returns, Payments. Notes stay, and stay 'just like customer'. Two of my own claims needed correcting first, by reading the templates rather than the sweep's summary.

NOTES — 'legacy' IS accurate, and the label is the only honest part of it. Company has NO plain notes column at all: the sell side has only threaded company_note rows, one per note with an author and a timestamp. Vendor has BOTH — the same threaded vendor_note rows AND an older single CLOB, and Vendor's own docblock says why: it 'stays as the record of what was written before there was anywhere better to put it'. So 'like customer' means ONE threaded list, not two boxes. The old column is not simply deleted: it may hold text a real person typed, so it is migrated into a vendor_note row (authored as a migration, dated) and only then removed. Dropping it would destroy the very thing it was kept for.

DB NAMES — the sweep said NINE and it is EIGHT. payment_term_id is inside a Twig {# #} comment in _vendor_fields.html.twig and never reaches the browser; I counted it from a grep without checking whether it rendered. The eight that do render are all inside <code> in explanatory prose, in two places: the address form's hint ('Codes, not names — vendor_address.province holds BC and .country holds CA') and the delete section's refusal ('Refused while any purchase_order.vendor_id, goods_receipt.vendor_id or vendor_bill.vendor_id names this row ... its own vendor_address, vendor_contact and vendor_note rows go with it'). This is not leakage of internals into a UI by accident — it is help text written in developer language. The fix is to rewrite the sentences, not to delete the explanation, which is genuinely useful: 'Can't delete a vendor that has purchase orders, receipts or bills — mark it Inactive instead. Deleting also removes its addresses, contacts and notes.'

Landed. Subtabs mirror the customer page; the old notes CLOB is MIGRATED into a vendor_note row rather than dropped, proven by bin/ci-migration-replay (72 migrations from empty, exit 0) with the assertion shown to bite by sabotaging the migration's WHERE and watching replay fail. items.title: No purchase document can be printed or sent, except a PO and an RFQ reply
items.detail: There is no way to produce or send a debit memo, a vendor return, a goods receipt or a vendor bill. Two of those matter: you raise a debit memo telling a vendor they owe you money and have no way to give it to them — they find out when you short-pay; and a vendor return sends goods out of the building with no paperwork for the box.
items.notes:
From the usability sweep, which enumerated every print and send route in the app. THE SAME GAP EXISTS ON THE SELL SIDE for the credit note and the sales return, so this is not a buy-side omission but a missing capability on both. The RFQ vendor reply gained a print screen today (item 16), which is the pattern to follow.

OWNER RULING (2026-09-12), and it is WIDER than the six documents I listed: "yes you need to do a full sweep. basically every doc has a pdf and print version. same button layouts." So this is not a priority order through six gaps — it is a capability every document has, proven by a sweep rather than by a list somebody maintains. Three consequences. (1) EVERY document gets both a print view and a PDF, buy side and sell side alike, including any added later. (2) The buttons are laid out identically on every document — a person learns the control once. (3) The gap is closed by a CONFORMANCE TEST that discovers documents and asserts each one has both, not by ticking off the six I happened to find; a hand-kept list of documents-with-print is the same anti-pattern docs/QUEUE.md already names. Note item 55 first: the test cannot discover through the CommercialDocument contract alone, because VendorReturn, Rfq and GoodsReceipt are deliberately outside it — and GoodsReceipt is one of the documents that needs printing. Settle 55's discovery route and this sweep rides on it.

items.notes:

So the deliverable is not the three findings — it is a line-by-line comparison of the bill screens against the invoice screens, with every difference either closed or argued. Item 15 is reopened alongside this, because it claimed exactly this work and I had it marked done. Do the comparison in BOTH directions and state it as a list: what invoice has that bill lacks, and what bill has that invoice lacks — the second half is how you avoid discovering later that the buy side was right about something. Known starting points, all three confirmed: add-another-line (the PO and RFQ forms already have it), a running total and subtotal, custom fees and taxes, and the heading that names the wrong table. items.title: The Edit button on the purchase order list works on 7 of 37 rows
items.detail: Every row offers Edit. Seven are Draft; the other thirty — Issued, Partially Received, Received, Closed, Cancelled — return 200 and render a fully editable form with a Save draft button, refusing only at save. No data changes, so the guard is real, but you find out after re-keying.
items.notes:
From the usability sweep. Compounding it: cancel is refused once anything has arrived, so an issued PO with a wrong price and one receipt against it has no correction path at all beyond closing it short. Offering an action that cannot succeed is the same defect class as the credit-note search box with no handler — the control is the promise.

OWNER RULING (2026-09-12). The easy half: hide Edit where it cannot work. The hard half is settled by BORROWING THE SELL SIDE, which the owner asked for directly and which turns out to already match what Zoho, NetSuite and Dynamics do.

WHAT THE SELL SIDE DOES, read from the code rather than assumed: OrderController::isOrderLockedForEditing() locks on Closed and Void ONLY, and its comment says the rest outright — 'An Invoiced order is deliberately NOT locked — a line can still be added to it, which is precisely how it becomes Partially Invoiced again.' It tracks SalesOrder::invoicedQuantityFor() and uninvoicedQuantityFor() per line, and InvoiceOrderMatcher refuses to invoice past ordered ('%s ordered, %s already invoiced').

THE BUY-SIDE RULE, ruled: (1) a purchase order locks for editing at CLOSED and CANCELLED only — Issued and Partially Received stay editable. (2) RECEIVED QUANTITY IS THE FLOOR: a line cannot go below what has arrived and a received line cannot be deleted. Owner: 'Can't delete a line if it's been received. But if nothing received then it's free to do whatever' and 'received is the floor. That's clear cut'. (3) PRICE IS CONSTRAINED BY BILLS, NOT RECEIPTS — they are different events. Receiving records that goods arrived and says nothing about what is owed; billing is where price becomes settled money. So a line received but not yet billed is still price-correctable, and a billed line is not, because the order would then disagree with a bill already accepted. This is what all three reference products do. (4) Cancel stays refused once anything is received — already settled earlier and reaffirmed here.

THE VARIANCE MACHINERY ALREADY EXISTS, which is why (3) costs little: ThreeWayMatchService runs a real PO/receipt/bill match, MatchLine carries a readonly priceVariance, and EXCEPTION_PRICE_VARIANCE is already one of the exception kinds beside EXCEPTION_BILLED_NOT_RECEIVED. So a bill arriving at a price the order did not expect is not a hard stop — it raises the price-variance exception that is already modelled. The bill's price is what you owe; the variance is the thing a buyer looks at.

UNVERIFIED, AND IT MUST BE CHECKED BEFORE COPYING: I could not find anything on the SELL side preventing a sales order line being REDUCED below what is already invoiced. The guard I found refuses invoicing past ordered, which is the opposite direction. A targeted grep finding nothing is not proof of absence, so this is recorded as a question rather than a defect — but if the hole is real, the buy side must not copy it, and the sell side needs the same floor. Check it first.

Landed. Locks at Closed and Cancelled only; received quantity floors a line and a received line cannot be removed; price is floored by BILLS through getQuantityCharged() — every bill but Draft and Void — deliberately not getQuantityBilled(), because a price somebody is mid-typing must not freeze the order it is typed against. Receipts and bills are never collapsed, proved by collapsing them and watching exactly one test fail by name.

THE PART THE ITEM DID NOT SEE, and shipping the lock alone would have been a silent data defect: the save deleted and rebuilt every line, and both goods_receipt_line and vendor_bill_line hold their line with ON DELETE SET NULL. The first edit of an issued order would have cut every receipt and bill loose from its line with no error, leaving the three-way match blind. Lines are diffed in place on their id now.

TWO SELL-SIDE FINDINGS, conducted on clean main. Reducing an invoiced order line below what is invoiced is ALLOWED — and that is deliberate, not a hole: SalesOrderStatusDeriverTest documents it by name, 'the excess already billed is a discrepancy to resolve with a credit', and states the policy that the invoice is the accounting record while the order is an operations document. But DELETING an invoiced line has no such defence and loses data: the line goes, and an invoice_line is left with sales_order_line_id NULL still billing the customer, so those units stop counting against anything. Core, frozen, reported not fixed — see item 63.

Verified targeted: new Cest 12/312 plus sixteen regression Cests, mutation-checked three ways.
