items.title: The bundles-off gate has never run the test that proves it is not a no-op
items.detail: BundlesOffEnvironmentCest executes in NEITHER gate. It is tagged @env bundles-off, so the ordinary suite reports 'No tests executed!' for it; and bin/ci-bundles-off runs `--env bundles-off -g bundle-agnostic`, which excludes it, because its own docblock says it cannot be tagged bundle-agnostic like the rest of the group. So the one test whose stated job is to prove the bundles-off harness is not silently a no-op — its own words: 'a false green is worse than no gate, because it stops anyone looking' — has itself never been executed. The fix is one more passthru in bin/ci-bundles-off without the -g filter.
items.notes: Found by the batch 6 merger while re-running after the catch-up, and it reported it rather than slipping it into the merge — correctly, it is a different script and was not in scope. It matters because feat/break-and-unbreak-a-case MODIFIED that Cest (2d0dc24c, the nav list gaining the pack-conversion screen) and the change was unverified until run by hand: `--env bundles-off` with no group filter gives OK (3 tests, 49 assertions), including a 404 proving the new screen disappears with the bundle off. So the branch is correct and the gate is blind. Same defect class as the PLAIN loophole: a check that cannot fail.
items.evidence: Already fixed on main (ce3a86fe) before this queue entry was actioned. Verified in both directions rather than re-fixed, in 8885122c. The real defect found while verifying: BundlesOffEnvironmentCest had a literal @env in its PROSE, which Codeception's annotation reader registered as a second bogus environment, printing "No tests executed!" warnings on every run of the gate.

items.title: The sidebar fixture is right, but its failure tells you nothing
items.detail: tests/Support/Fixtures/admin_default_sidebar_nav.html is compared byte for byte, and on failure it emits a ~28KB expected-versus-actual string diff of one line of HTML. That is how a one-row difference got misdiagnosed twice in one evening, including by me asserting a docs-only commit could not reach the menu when TechnicalDocsBundle publishes every docs/**.md as a nav row.
items.notes:
The merger's recommendation, and it argued down the obvious answer: do NOT add a second check that re-encodes the same coupling, which is the hand-kept-list anti-pattern QUEUE.md names this very fixture for. Three pieces, in value order. (1) Keep the byte assertion; on failure diff the two navs into rows by label and href and report only the symmetric difference — 'the rendered sidebar has 1 row the fixture does not: DECISIONS-NEEDED -> /admin/technical-docs/view/DECISIONS-NEEDED.md'. One line instead of 28KB, a message change with no rule change. (2) When the differing rows sit under Technical Docs, append that those rows come from a recursive Finder over docs/*.md, so adding or removing a markdown file there changes this sidebar — refresh the fixture in the same commit (precedent 77c15a4b, 89ceba61) or keep the file outside docs/. That sentence is exactly what was rediscovered twice. (3) A millisecond PHPUnit guard derived from BOTH sides rather than hand-kept: assert DocsRepository::list() and the Technical Docs rows in the committed fixture are the same set, failing with 'docs/X.md exists but the fixture has no row for it'. No HTTP, no Codeception, and it catches this for someone running only PHPUnit, which is the cheap loop most people run first. OWNER QUESTION, on the decision sheet: docs/ currently means both 'reference material admins should see' and 'the repo's own working notes', and only the first belongs in a nav. Excluding a subtree (docs/notes/**) would remove the class of problem instead of improving its error message.

OWNER RULING (2026-09-12) on the docs/ question this item raised: "tech support only. No one else can see. Answer is yes." So the fix is neither of the two options I offered — it is PERMISSION, not path filtering. The whole Technical Docs section is gated to tech support and is invisible to every other admin. That dissolves the docs/ subtree question: if only support can see it, plans and code reviews sitting beside real reference material stops mattering.

CONSEQUENCES TO HANDLE. (1) The DEFAULT sidebar no longer carries Technical Docs rows at all, so tests/Support/Fixtures/admin_default_sidebar_nav.html changes — regenerate it from a real render, and prove the edit by asserting the anchor occurred exactly once and that undoing it returns the file byte for byte. AdminMenuDefaultSidebarCest arbitrates, 3 tests, 0.7s, 64MB, no test slot needed. (2) It also largely removes the cause this item exists for: once the default sidebar has no docs rows, adding a markdown file under docs/ stops changing that fixture, which is the trap that misdiagnosed twice in one evening. The diagnostic improvements are still worth building — a one-line symmetric-difference message beats a 28KB string diff regardless — but the coupling note (2) and the PHPUnit set guard (3) should be re-judged against a permission-gated section rather than built as originally specified. (3) The ROUTE must be gated too, not just the menu row: a hidden link whose URL still serves to anyone is not 'no one else can see'. (4) Check what 'tech support' means here — whether a role already exists or one is being introduced — and say which.
items.evidence: Already built on main (ce3a86fe). Re-proven in 8885122c with a planted docs/zzz-planted.md: the one-line symmetric-difference message and the Technical Docs coupling sentence both fire as designed, and the PHPUnit guard names the file.

items.title: A status has no declared colour, so every new one silently lands on the default
items.detail: Colour is decided in CSS by matching a status slug, so a status nobody wrote a rule for renders slate like every other. That is how Accepted, Rejected, Declined, Voided, Open and Authorised came to have no colour of their own, and Issued, Received, Disputed, Partially Paid, Priced and Submitted still have none. Nothing fails when a new status is added; it just quietly looks like everything else.
items.notes:
Raised by the item 41 agent when asked for a recommendation, NOT built — this needs an owner ruling and is on the decision sheet. Two parts, and the second matters more than the first.

THE MECHANISM (the valuable half): each status enum DECLARES its category through a tone() method returning one of a fixed set of tokens, rather than CSS inferring it from a slug. A conformance test then asserts every enum case names one, the way EveryDocumentDeclaresItsContractTest already does for documents. That is what stops the next status landing on the default in silence. The palette is cosmetic; this is not.

THE PALETTE: four categories, and the agent argues four is the FLOOR, because a status is scanned rather than read and the reader is asking two binary questions — is this finished, and did it go wrong. (1) NOT YET REAL, grey: Draft, Invited. (2) LIVE, WAITING ON SOMEONE, amber: Pending, Approved, Issued, Sent, Open, On Hold, Requested, Authorised, Submitted, Priced, Replied and every Partially-* state — this is the work queue. (3) DONE CORRECTLY, green: Closed, Completed, Received, Paid, Invoiced, Accepted, Credited. (4) DEAD OR WRONG, red: Cancelled, Void, Voided, Rejected, Declined, Expired, Disputed. Three categories loses the grey/green split, which is the one distinction a grid is actually scanned for.

The only real change to what exists today is folding the current blue 'in progress' tier (Processing, Invoiced) into amber, on the argument that 'how far along is it' is a question you ask after opening the row, not while scanning. The one contestable placement is DISPUTED — red by outcome, amber by workload; if the owner wants a fifth category it is that one, outlined rather than filled. The owner has said not to spend tokens on artwork, so this is deliberately a ruling on categories and mechanism, not on hues.

THE OWNER HAS NOW RULED THE MECHANISM, on item 42, before reaching this item: colour classes are shared, core CSS defines every class it knows of, and objects sharing a trait get identical treatment. That settles the half of this item I called the valuable half — it is not per-status hues scattered across templates, it is a core-owned trait vocabulary. What remains open here is only how many categories that vocabulary needs and where Disputed sits.

OWNER RULING (2026-09-12): "whatever is fine that's a 1 line css change" — the palette is delegated, so FOUR categories, and Disputed sits in RED. No fifth category. grey = not real yet (Draft, Invited); amber = live and waiting on someone (Pending, Approved, Issued, Sent, Open, On Hold, Requested, Authorised, Submitted, Priced, Replied and every Partially-* state); green = done correctly (Closed, Completed, Received, Paid, Invoiced, Accepted, Credited); red = dead or wrong (Cancelled, Void, Voided, Rejected, Declined, Expired, Disputed). The existing blue in-progress tier (Processing, Invoiced) folds into amber.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE OWNER'S FRAMING, recorded because building it as a one-line CSS change would reproduce the defect: the PALETTE is one line, but the MECHANISM is not, and their own item 42 ruling already requires it. Colour is currently matched off a slugified status string in CSS, so a status nobody wrote a rule for renders slate and nothing notices — that is how Accepted and Rejected lost their colour in the first place, by omission rather than decision. The fix is each status enum DECLARING its category (a tone() method returning one of the four tokens) with a conformance test asserting every case of every status enum names one, discovered from the enums themselves rather than a hand-kept list, the way EveryDocumentDeclaresItsContractTest works. Without that, the next status added silently goes grey again.

MEASURED COST of folding blue into amber, so nobody is surprised: .order-status-processing and .order-status-invoiced are var(--admin-blue) #408dfb today. Invoiced is a SalesOrderStatus and renders on the /admin/order grid, the order detail hero badge and the order edit pill; Processing is an InvoiceStatus and renders on the /admin/invoice grid, the invoice detail Info card and the invoices table on every order detail page. The visible effect is that the order grid stops distinguishing 'approved, not yet invoiced' from 'invoiced, awaiting close' at a glance — both become amber alongside Partially Invoiced.

items.title: The vendor return list is outside the reach of the list-conventions rule
items.detail: The vendor returns list gained a second flat row control in batch 7 and NOTHING caught it. AdminListScreenConventionsCest discovers the grids it polices through documentGrids(), which is scoped to the CommercialDocument contract — and VendorReturn deliberately is not a CommercialDocument. Rfq and GoodsReceipt are outside it for the same reason. So three real document lists are invisible to the rule that is supposed to keep document lists consistent, and a screen can drift with no test objecting.
items.notes: Found and recorded by the batch 7 merger in b043e805, which correctly refused to fix it inside a merge: widening the contract is a design decision, not a conflict resolution. Two shapes are possible and they are not equivalent. Either VendorReturn, Rfq and GoodsReceipt become CommercialDocuments — which changes what the contract MEANS, since they are excluded on purpose — or the conventions test discovers its grids by some route other than that contract, for instance every admin list route that renders a .table-card. The second keeps the contract honest and is probably right, but it widens the rule's reach to screens nobody has audited, so it should land with its offenders argued as entries the way KNOWN_OFFENDERS and PLAIN_LISTS already do rather than as a big bang.

items.title: Hide the RFQ screens until the tender model is built properly
items.detail: The RFQ is half a tender and the owner does not want it on screen in that state: "We can hide our half ass Rfq for now." Hide the sidebar entry and every entry point that leads to RFQ creation. DELETE NOTHING — Rfq, RfqLine, RfqVendorReply, RfqVendorReplyLine, their controllers, templates, routes and tests all stay in the repository, because GitHub #662 builds on them. Any RFQ rows already in a database stay reachable by their own URL rather than 404-ing; this is a removal from the menu, not a removal of the feature.
items.notes:
Why it is being hidden rather than finished: RfqConversionService::convert() takes one whole RfqVendorReply and produces one purchase order, so a single vendor wins everything, and it refuses unless isFullyPriced(), so a vendor quoting only the lines they stock cannot win at all. NetSuite awards PER LINE — 'check the box in the Award column to award that line item', with different vendors winning different lines — and Zoho likewise awards items to vendors of your choice. Splitting an award is what tendering is for, so what is built is not a small gap.

WATCH THE SIDEBAR FIXTURE: tests/Support/Fixtures/admin_default_sidebar_nav.html is compared byte for byte and removing a nav row WILL change it. Regenerate it from a real render, and prove the edit the way the three-way merge was proved — the anchor occurs exactly once, and undoing the edit returns the file byte for byte. AdminMenuDefaultSidebarCest arbitrates and runs in 0.7s at 64MB, so it needs no test slot. Also check whether hiding this changes the bundle's landing page counts or the App Management descriptor.
items.evidence: GitHub #662

items.title: The sidebar fixture is not compared byte for byte, though everyone believes it is
items.detail: AdminMenuDefaultSidebarCest::normalize() strips all inter-tag whitespace from BOTH sides before assertSame. It is equivalent to a byte comparison today only because the committed fixture happens to be a single 27,945-byte line with no inter-tag whitespace, so normalize() is a no-op on it. The moment anyone regenerates that file with a renderer that emits whitespace between tags — or hand-edits it — the guarantee silently weakens: a change that only altered whitespace would pass. The Cest's own docblock argues at length for why matching raw bytes was deliberately rejected, so the normalisation is intentional; what is wrong is that everyone working on it, me included, has been briefing and reasoning as though it were byte-exact.
items.notes:
Found by the agent hiding the RFQ menu row, which proved byte equality anyway — stronger than the test actually asks for — and then said plainly that my brief was wrong about the mechanism. Worth deciding rather than leaving as folklore, because the belief is load-bearing: several briefs tonight told agents to prove fixture edits 'byte for byte', and they complied against a test that does not require it. Either make the assertion match the belief, or make the docblock and the surrounding guidance match the assertion — but the two should not disagree.

A RELATED STALENESS from the same agent, not a separate item: docs/QUEUE.md still says '1 slot on the current 3.9 GB box'. The box is 16 GB and bin/test-slot yields 3 slots at SUITE_PEAK_MB 4000. Agents size their plans around that sentence, so it is two hardware generations of wrong guidance sitting in the file that is supposed to be authoritative. Same failure mode as the ci-bundles-off docblock corrected earlier tonight, where a stale measurement was quoted back at an agent as a live constraint.
items.evidence: Done in 8885122c. Ruling taken: the normalisation STAYS and the folklore was corrected instead. Fixture measured at 27,847 bytes on one line with zero inter-tag whitespace runs, so normalize() is an accidental no-op — the equivalence to a byte comparison is a coincidence, not a rule. Wording corrected in AdminMenuDefaultSidebarCest, SidebarNavRows, SidebarNavRowsTest and docs/QUEUE.md. Also corrected two stale numbers in QUEUE.md that agents were sizing plans around (box is 16 GB not 3.9 GB; bin/test-slot yields 3 slots) and made that file say what bin/test-slot IS and when it is needed.

items.title: Moving a payment between invoices leaves the losing invoice saying Paid with no payments
items.detail: On the sell side, InvoicePaymentStatusSubscriber::queueFromEntity() reads $payment->getInvoice(), which after a move is the TARGET. A payment leaving an invoice is not a change to the invoice row — addLog() puts the new log in collectionUpdates and never puts the invoice in entityUpdates — so the SOURCE invoice is never queued for recalculation. Proven by probe, not inferred: re-pointing an InvoicePayment from invoice A to invoice B through the public surface and flushing moves the row and keeps its id (invoice_id 1->2, id stays 1), B correctly becomes Paid, and A is STILL Paid while holding zero payments.
items.notes: Found by the item 34 agent while working out what the sell side would need; it ran a throwaway probe and deleted it rather than assuming. THIS IS LIVE ON MAIN TODAY and is not introduced by the payment-move feature — anything that re-points an InvoicePayment hits it. The fix belongs in the subscriber, at onFlush, checking $uow->getEntityChangeSet($payment)['invoice'] and queueing the OLD invoice as well as the new. It does NOT belong at a call site: the subscriber is the single writer of derived payment status and keeping it that way is the whole point of the design. Core, so the freeze applies. Note the buy side has no such listener at all — VendorBillStatusDeriver::recalculate() is called by hand at every call site — which is a declared asymmetry, not a second instance of this bug.

items.title: A draft invoice can still book payments: the guard is on an unmerged branch, not on main
items.detail: Invoice::recordPayment() refuses only Cancelled. InvoiceController::payments() and savePayment() have no status check at all, and the template gates only on invoice.cancelled. So a draft invoice accepts payments on main right now. InvoiceStatus::acceptsPayment(), the guard that fixes it, exists ONLY on the unmerged branch fix/sell-side-double-invoicing.
items.notes:
The owner ruled on this directly: "that's a no-no. how can a draft invoice book payments against it? jesus lol pls guard against it. the view draft should not have any book payments screen and yes guard it." I then told a later agent the guard was already in place, and it checked and corrected me: it is not on main. Item 33's notes already say 'Once that lands', so the dependency was recorded — what was wrong was my summary of the current state. Two ways to close it: land fix/sell-side-double-invoicing (which carries acceptsPayment()), or guard it directly. The owner's ruling asks for BOTH halves — the draft's payments screen should not be offered at all, AND the save path must refuse — because hiding a screen whose POST still works is not a guard. Core, so the freeze applies.

DONE, closed by the same branch that closed item 31. Both halves the owner demanded are present: the Payments tab, the detail link, the order-screen link and the list row-action are all withheld from a draft, AND InvoiceStatus::acceptsPayment() refuses the POST in the controller and again in Invoice::recordPayment() — because hiding a screen whose POST still works is not a guard.

Landed at main bc117713's successor. Verified targeted on both trees at the same base: Codeception 129/1653 -> 143/2146, PHPUnit 234/815 -> 236/823, all exit 0, the deltas being exactly this branch's two new Cests and two new unit tests. No migration, replay not applicable.

items.title: An issued invoice can be linked to an order after the fact, with the refusal in the wrong place
items.detail: Invoice::linkToOrder() checks no status, so an already-issued standalone invoice can be attached to an order after it was issued — a second door onto the same order line. The door is not actually open: InvoiceOrderMatcher computes each line's remainder from uninvoicedQuantityFor() and reports a blocking mismatch. But the refusal lives in the MATCHER, not on the entity, which is the opposite of the arrangement item 31 just argued for everywhere else — the rule should sit where the state changes, not in whatever happens to be reading it.
items.notes: Pre-existing, from #539 stage 5, and NOT widened by item 31's work — reported by the agent that landed it rather than fixed in passing, which was right. Worth doing because item 31's whole argument is that a guard belongs at the moment state changes and must be unreachable around: transitionTo() private, no setStatus(). This is the one remaining path into the same quantity that does not follow that shape.

items.title: A warehouse created from a fulfillment region has no province, so its purchase orders compute zero tax
items.detail: WarehouseFulfillmentRegionService::createWarehouseForRegion() builds a Warehouse from a name and a status and nothing else — and it CANNOT do better, because FulfillmentRegion carries no province, country or city at all. Item 37 then made a purchase order derive its tax province from its warehouse. So every warehouse created through that path yields a null province, no calculator claims the document, and the tax comes out 0.00 — a zero derived from nothing, which is indistinguishable on the document from a genuine zero. That is the exact failure item 37 was written to close, arriving through the door item 37 did not check.
items.notes:
Found because it turned main RED: PurchaseOrderChargesAndTaxCest failed 7 of 13 with tax 0.00 where 4.00 was expected. The agent landing item 47 reported it and correctly said it was not theirs; I reproduced it on clean main before touching anything. Main is green again — the fixture's warehouse now says it is in Alberta, which is honest for a test that prices Alberta tax — but THE FIXTURE WAS NOT THE DEFECT, it only exposed it.

What is still open: a real warehouse created from a region is in the same state as that fixture was, so its purchase orders price at zero. Item 37's guard refuses to ISSUE a taxable order whose province is unknown, so the money never leaves on bad paperwork — but a draft will sit there quoting zero tax until someone tries, and 'be clear and be loud' says that should be visible at the point the draft is written, not only at the gate.

Three possible answers, all owner calls. Give FulfillmentRegion a province and have the factory copy it — but a region is a delivery area and may legitimately span provinces, so that may be wrong. Refuse to create a warehouse without an address at all. Or leave creation alone and make the missing province loud on the warehouse screen and on every draft that inherits it. Note item 32 gave Warehouse its address precisely so this fact would live in one place; nothing made the existing rows fill it in.

OWNER RULING (2026-09-12): "warehouse should NOT have province empty at creation or edit." So of the three options recorded above, it is the second — REFUSE TO CREATE OR SAVE A WAREHOUSE WITHOUT A PROVINCE — and the other two are dropped. A fulfillment region does not gain a province (it is a delivery area and may legitimately span several), and making the gap merely loud is not enough when the fact is always knowable: a building is somewhere.

THE HARD PART IS NOT THE VALIDATION, IT IS createWarehouseForRegion(). That factory builds a Warehouse from a region's name and status and cannot supply a province, because FulfillmentRegion carries none. So it must either take one as an argument or stop creating warehouses implicitly — and every caller has to be found and answered. That decision belongs with whoever does the work; both are legitimate and the callers decide which.

EXISTING ROWS: a required field on a table that already holds rows without it is the interesting half. Whatever lands must say what happens to warehouses that exist today with a null province — they cannot simply start failing to save. The honest shapes are a migration that fills them from somewhere real, or a screen that refuses to save until the gap is answered while still letting the row be loaded and read.

DONE. The factory demands province and country and throws; of its five callers the three that cannot honestly name a province now REFUSE to create a warehouse rather than guess. That split turned on a real temptation: there IS a system-wide company province, and defaulting to it would stamp BC on a CSV row reading 'Toronto DC' and compute GST-only on an Ontario building forever. A wrong province is worse than a missing one — the missing one is refused at item 37's gate, the wrong one is believed.

COUNTRY WAS REQUIRED TOO, on evidence: resolveProvinceAnyCountry('CA') returns CALIFORNIA, because Canada has no province CA and the US has a state CA. It resolves, passes every guard, and then no calculator claims a US state and the tax is 0.00. Typing the country into the province box reproduced this very item's defect through item 37's own gate.

TWO MORE DEFECTS, same root cause: ConfigController's 'is not a province or state code' branch could never fire, and Warehouse::setProvince() stored 'XX' while its docblock promised null.

NO MIGRATION, and my brief was wrong to offer one: docs/QUEUE.md forbids writing to existing data in any environment, so the backfill option never existed. Null rows stay loadable and editable, marked on the list, warned on arrival at the form, refused only at save.

97 test call sites across 77 files gained the arguments, so the fixture universe now matches the rule.

items.title: Document list rows are two lines tall because body cells wrap, costing 2-3 rows on every list
items.detail: Measured in a real browser at 1366x900: the shared chrome takes 374px of the 852px clamp (59 admin header, 108 title panel, 95 sticky thead, 95 filter bar, 69 footer) and what is left divides by a 66px row. That 66px is TWO LINES — '2026-09-12' breaks at its hyphens and 'CAD 3,296.54' at its space. Stopping body cells wrapping gives 8 rows at rest and 9 once the filter bar scrolls away, on EVERY document list, from one rule.
items.notes:
Reported rather than taken by the item 46 agent, and its reasoning is why this needs an owner: nowrap on a .table-card body cell is a trait core already names THREE TIMES LOCALLY — .company-table td, .user-manager-table td, .settings-table td — and never generally. A fourth local name is exactly the invention the item 42 colour ruling forbids, so the fix is one general rule in core CSS, which is frozen.

ALSO MEASURED AND WORTH KNOWING: item 41 COST every procurement screen 52px of scroll region. Unhiding .lead inside .panel-title-row made the bundle title panel taller, measured at 602px -> 550px between two runs on the same screen. That is a real cost of a ruling the owner made deliberately and would still make — status must be visible — but it makes this item worth more than it was yesterday.

The right generalisation is a sixth compositional rule in AdminListScreenConventionsCest. It cannot land today: it would fail on four screens that are mid-flight, and the only way to green would be KNOWN_OFFENDERS entries, which is forbidden. It lands when they are conformed.

items.title: Deleting an invoiced sales order line orphans its invoice line and the units stop counting
items.detail: Conducted on clean main through the real screens: an order line of 10 invoiced for 4, then the line deleted — the line goes, and one invoice_line is left with sales_order_line_id NULL. The invoice still bills the customer for 4 units, but invoicedQuantityFor() attributes by that foreign key, so those 4 stop counting against anything. src/Controller/Admin/OrderController.php:722-731 is the removal loop.
items.notes:
Found by the item 47 agent while checking whether the buy side should copy the sell side's behaviour, and it correctly separated two things I had lumped together. REDUCING an invoiced line below what is invoiced is deliberate and documented — SalesOrderStatusDeriverTest names it: 'the excess already billed is a discrepancy to resolve with a credit', on the policy that the invoice is the accounting record and the order is an operations document. So that half is a considered position, not a hole, and the buy side's stricter floor is a deliberate divergence rather than a correction.

DELETING has no such defence. It silently detaches money that was already billed. Core, so the freeze applies and it was reported rather than fixed.

Related, and the same shape: on the BUY side, item 47 allows removing a billed-but-unreceived line, because the owner's rule is that receipts floor a line and an unreceived line is free. That orphans vendor_bill_line.purchase_order_line_id exactly as this does. No refusal was invented; it was made LOUD — the timeline entry names the line and says N units of it are on a vendor bill which now charges against no order line. Whether that should instead be refused, on both sides, is an owner call. The same question applies to swapping the product on a received line.

items.title: Status is a declared, dynamically loaded vocabulary — not a method per value
items.detail: Three operations on the seam: getStatus, setStatus, and a verify/validity check. Behind them a DYNAMIC LOADER supplying the status definitions — slugs, labels, and which transitions are legal. It reads a hardcoded config array to begin with, and the point of the loader is that the array can later be replaced by a database or per-tenant configuration WITHOUT touching a single call site.
items.notes:
OWNER RULING (2026-09-12), and it overrules my objection to setStatus — correctly. I argued a public setStatus() re-opens the door the product form walked through. That is only true of an UNGUARDED setter: if it consults the declared transition map, the guard moves from the method NAME into the DECLARATION, which is the only place it can be made configurable. Owner: "it should be set status, get status, verify status ... and yes it needs A DYNAMIC LOADER SO IT OPENS THE PATH FOR CUSTOM STATUSES IN THE FUTURE. Right now it can dynamically load from a hard code config array but we can easily replace that in the future."

WHY THE CURRENT DESIGN LOSES THIS ARGUMENT, stated plainly because I defended it too long. Today the legal moves live INSIDE method bodies, so nothing can ask a document what it may do next — and every screen therefore hand-maintains its own copy of that knowledge. That is not hypothetical: item 47 was the Edit button rendering on 37 rows and succeeding on 7, and the product form's hand-kept ['Active','Inactive'] list silently activated drafts. Both are the same defect as a hand-kept list, which docs/QUEUE.md already names as the anti-pattern. A declared map makes the UI DERIVE what is legal instead of re-implementing it in Twig.

WHAT THE VERBS ARE STILL FOR, and it is a genuinely smaller set than today's: a verb earns its place only where there is a real SIDE EFFECT, not merely a status change. issue() freezes the vendor snapshot and the address so renaming a vendor cannot rewrite an old order; void() on a debit memo writes an inventory adjustment and offers three outcomes; approve() on a bill refuses taxable goods with no province on file. Those are operations that happen to end in a status change, not status changes wearing a name. Everything that is only a status change goes through setStatus and the map.

WHAT ELSE HANGS OFF THE SAME REGISTRY once it exists: labels (so no template spells a status by hand), item 54's tone() for colour, and the INITIAL state — which today is ten entities each hardcoding `= XStatus::Draft` in a field initialiser, the same hand-rolled pattern in a place nobody looks.

SCOPE NOTE: this is not only CommercialDocument. ProductCore, Company and Warehouse are not documents and are exactly where the free-string statuses live — 20 of them against 10 enum-typed. The seam wants to be a HasStatus that CommercialDocument requires, not something only documents get.

DECIDED SO FAR (2026-09-12, owner, in discussion — several points still open at the bottom).

(a) IT IS ITS OWN INTERFACE, BUILT NOW. `HasStatus` holds the methods and `CommercialDocument` EXTENDS it. The owner's argument won and it is the better call: it is about fifty lines, status is not a document concept (a product, a warehouse and a user each have one), and building it separately now costs the same as extracting it later. I had argued for putting it on CommercialDocument and deferring — wrong, because 'prove it first' applies to the loader and the transition map, which are the expensive risky parts, not to where five signatures live. Master data implements it opportunistically when somebody is next in that file; no coordinated migration.

(b) FIVE METHODS: getStatus, setStatus, canTransitionTo (the owner's 'verify'), listStatuses (the whole vocabulary), allowedTransitions (legal from the CURRENT state). The last two are deliberately not one method: a filter bar wants all six statuses, a detail screen wants 'you may Issue or Cancel'. Collapsing them means every screen filters the list itself, which is the hand-rolled knowledge being removed. 'Is this a known status' needs no method — it falls out of listStatuses().

(c) setStatus ALWAYS RETURNS A STATUS. Owner: "we have a duty to return status at all times" — not void, not bool. A bool can be ignored silently, which is the fail-silently the owner banned. On an ILLEGAL MOVE it THROWS, and the owner's condition is exact: "a throw works for me (as long as its caught)". So every user-facing path must CATCH it and render the message — an uncaught DomainException is a 500, which is the opposite of clear and loud. This matches the house style: deriveTaxProvinceFrom() and Rfq::cancel() already throw with messages a person can read.

(d) SHAPE ONLY. Owner, emphatically: no status is renamed and no value changes. Processing and On Hold stay on InvoiceStatus. Void and Cancelled keep their current inconsistent usage. What is legal today stays legal — it just becomes declared instead of buried in method bodies.

(e) THE CONSEQUENCE OF CUSTOM STATUSES, raised and not yet ruled: PHP enums are compiled, so a customer can never add a case from a UI. If custom statuses are a real goal then the LOADER is the source of truth for slugs, labels and transitions, the stored column stays a plain string (it already is), and any enum that survives is only the BUILT-IN set — a convenience for code that prefers InvoiceStatus::Draft to 'Draft', not the authority. That inverts what I proposed earlier, where the enum was authoritative.

STILL OPEN: whether the enums stay as the built-in set or go entirely; the shape of the define/loader method; whether listStatuses is static (a filter bar has no document in hand) or instance; and where the initial state comes from, since today it is ten entities each hardcoding `= XStatus::Draft` in a field initialiser.

items.title: PARKED FOR DISCUSSION: the back-office walkthrough's findings, none of them ruled
items.detail: A worker took the persona of a back-office worker at a distribution business, was given no guidance and told not to read source, and drove the whole flow: ten products on ten different tracking policies, a purchase order, a vendor bill, a goods receipt, a quote, a sales order and an invoice. It got from an empty catalogue to an invoiced sale, with seven workarounds nothing told it to make, and one leg it could not do at all. NOTHING HERE IS RULED. It is parked whole, for the owner to work through when they have room for it — they asked for it to be queued rather than acted on.
items.blocked_by: needs an owner discussion, not a dispatch
items.notes:
REPRODUCIBLE: tests/Functional/WarehouseToInvoiceWalkthroughCest.php on branch test/end-to-end-ten-skus — one file, 1898 lines, no production code touched, 22 tests / 3381 assertions, ~5 minutes. It writes the stock table to tests/_output/walkthrough.log. Re-run it before discussing; several findings below are the kind that get fixed by accident.

COULD NOT BE DONE AT ALL — receiving serial-tracked goods. The typed receipt form correctly demands one line per serial, and renders exactly one row per purchase order line with no control to add another. The scan console refuses serials and says in its own words that such a product 'has to be booked in on the typed form, where the field is there and is enforced'. Each screen sends you to the other. And the scanner's claim is false: the typed form enforces one-unit-per-serial IF you type a serial, and never asks for one. So the only way to get serialised stock onto the shelf is to leave the serial blank — the exact outcome tracking exists to prevent. The agent's framing is right: this needs DECIDING, not patching. Either the receipt form grows an add-line control and bulk serial entry, or the scanner captures serials, or the policy stops offering serial tracking. Any one is fine; all three at once is what exists.

RULES PRINTED BUT NOT ENFORCED — the class of defect that teaches people to ignore your messages. (1) The bill screen states 'A bill with taxable goods and no province cannot be approved.' Pressing Approve for payment moved it Draft -> Open, with the sentence still on screen. (2) Filling in the warehouse address does not clear it: the same screen then prints 'Received at Main — 1 Walkthrough Way, Surrey, BC, V3S 0A1' TWO LINES ABOVE the sentence saying the warehouse has no province on file. (3) With a purchase order loaded the goods receipt form has no required field at all — confirmed with a positive control that the same screen without a PO does mark vendor and warehouse required. 550 units across ten SKUs, six of which capture an identity inbound, every box blank, nothing objected. (4) A batch and a serial can be typed against a product whose policy captures neither; the boxes are identical on every line. (5) A policy flagged 'the batch must carry an expiry date' produced a batch with no expiry, and the Lots screen prints 'Does not expire'.

THE EXCEPTIONS SCREEN CONTRADICTS THE BILL SCREEN. Bill detail said '10 exception(s). Every one needs a human.' At the same moment Procurement > Exceptions said 'No bill exceptions. Every bill matches its purchase order and its receipts, within tolerance.' It counts only APPROVED bills and says so nowhere. Anyone working that screen as their queue never sees a draft bill's problems.

THREE REFERENCE LISTS THAT DO NOT EXIST UNTIL SOMEBODY BROWSES TO THEM — Tracking Policies, Fulfillment Regions, Units of Measure. Each is created the first time its config screen is opened, and every screen that depends on one renders a half-form and says nothing: Add Product shows NO tracking policy field and a U/M select with zero options; quoting is refused with 'Activate a fulfillment region for this customer' and no way to do it. Consequences actually hit: the first ten products saved with no unit of measure, so every downstream line prints '-'. And two screens flatly contradicted each other — Customer Fulfillment Regions said 'No customer/region assignments found' while Add Product was offering opening-stock boxes for all three regions. A fourth prerequisite (a Pricing Group) surfaced only by being refused: 'Select a price list before activating Main'. The agent's verdict is the one to read: a careful inventory engine behind a setup process that quietly fails will make new installs look broken to people who blame themselves.

ACCEPTING A QUOTE RAISES THE INVOICE. 'Accept on behalf of customer' produced a sales order already in status Invoiced with INV-1 attached — no invoice date, no number, no choice about billing in full, and no warning on the quote screen. In this trade that is a document that goes to a customer and into the ledger. It is also why Sales Hold is permanently empty: its tooltip says 'committed to accepted orders and not yet billed', and that moment never exists.

ONLY THREE TRACKING IDENTITIES EXIST, not the ten the brief assumed: None, Lot (batch and lot are one thing), Serial. Expiry is a tick-box meaningful only on Lot. Ten DISTINCT POLICIES were built from the two direction flags plus expiry — including one the form allowed that captures nothing at all (Lot, both directions unticked), which is None wearing another name. The new-policy form's DEFAULT state is Identity = None with 'capture it on the way in' pre-ticked: a meaningless combination shipped as the default. The Tracking Policy select also offers both 'Not set — nothing captured' and 'None — No identity captured'.

BILL-BEFORE-RECEIVE vs RECEIVE-BEFORE-BILL, both run: stock figures byte-identical, because billing touches no inventory bucket. The only difference is the three-way match — bill first gives 10 exceptions, receive first gives zero. So the sequence generates the entire exception queue, which is correct behaviour and worth knowing is that sensitive to data-entry order.

WHAT WORKS, CREDITED, because it should not be lost in a defect list. Availability RECONCILED AT EVERY STEP against every visible column and its stated sign, in all three warehouses, and the grid shows its arithmetic in the Available tooltip ('10 - 2 = 8'). The Tracking Worklist behaved exactly as designed: after receiving with nothing captured it listed exactly the six SKUs whose policy captures an identity inbound, correctly excluding None, both out-only policies and the capture-nothing one. Oversell protection held the order as a Draft reserving nothing, with a per-line explanation carrying real numbers. The three-way match on bill detail is right. The explanatory copy throughout is genuinely good — which makes the gaps stranger, not more forgivable.

SMALLER, ALL REAL: money and quantity formatting inconsistent within a single row (Ordered 10, Outstanding 10.00, Unit cost 1.5, Subtotal 15; header 'CAD 5040' and 'Balance CAD 5040.00' four lines apart); document status is one segment of a run-on line with no label of its own; a new purchase order gives exactly five line rows and no add-a-line control, so ten SKUs took two passes; Pricing Group defaults to USD in an app whose provinces, taxes and vendor default are Canadian; a business customer's name is split into a person's first and last name; Expected Arrivals lists orders rather than products, so it cannot answer 'how many of this SKU are coming'; the invoice list explains itself wrongly ('Invoices are raised from an order's Convert to Invoice' — this one was not); the inventory grid has no tracking column, so you cannot tell serial-tracked from untracked while looking at stock; and the oversell success flash says only 'order SO-1 has been created' with nothing about it being held.

CORRECTIONS TO WHAT I HAD RECORDED: reservedQuantity DOES have a writer — saving a product through the product form forces it to 0 — so 'no writer anywhere' was wrong even though the effect is the same. And THREE columns are excluded from availability, not one: reserved, incoming and manual_adjustment all carry sign 0, and the grid labels all three 'not counted'.

TWO PROCESS NOTES. The agent read source for roughly the first third before the brief changed to black-box, said so unprompted, and flagged the two findings it would not have made otherwise. And: Codeception reuses a single Cest instance across methods, so per-run state leaked between tests and produced 15 spurious failures that looked like real defects — a trap for anyone writing multi-method Cests here.

items.title: A fully addressed US warehouse computes zero tax, because no calculator claims a US state
items.detail: After item 61 a US warehouse is perfectly legal: country US, province CA resolves cleanly to California, and it passes PurchaseOrder::assertTaxProvinceKnownIfTaxable() and VendorBill::approve(). Then TaxBCBundle and TaxCanadaSimpleBundle are the only calculators, neither claims a US state, and the tax comes out 0.00. Same 'zero derived from nothing' shape as item 61 — reached this time through a warehouse that is fully and honestly addressed.
items.notes:
Reported rather than fixed by the item 61 agent, and its reasoning is why: refusing US provinces at the address screen would be wrong, because this is a TAX-COVERAGE question and not an address question. The warehouse is telling the truth; the app has no calculator for where it is.

So the decision is what the app should do when a document's province resolves to a jurisdiction no installed calculator covers. Options, all owner calls: refuse to issue such a document the way a missing province is refused; allow it but state on the document that no tax rule applies to this jurisdiction, which is the honest reading of a genuine zero; or treat it as a prompt to install a calculator. What it must NOT do is what it does now, which is print 0.00 indistinguishable from a real zero — the exact defect item 37 exists to close.

items.title: Serial-tracked goods have no way onto the shelf
items.detail: Neither receiving screen can capture a serial, and each points at the other. The TYPED receipt form correctly demands one line per serial — 'so it is a line for one unit. Enter 10 separate lines of 1, each with its own serial' — and then renders exactly one row per purchase order line with NO control to add another, and one submit button. So it demands ten lines on a screen that can give you one. The SCAN CONSOLE refuses serials outright, in its own words: 'Batch codes, expiry dates and serials are not asked for here. A product whose receiving rules require one has to be booked in on the typed form, where the field is there and is enforced.' That claim is FALSE — the typed form enforces one-unit-per-serial only IF you type a serial, and never asks for one. The only way to get serialised stock onto the shelf today is to leave the serial blank, which is precisely the outcome tracking exists to prevent.
items.notes:
OWNER RULING (2026-09-12): build it on BOTH screens. I had offered 'stop offering serial tracking' as one of three options and the owner rejected it outright — serial tracking is table stakes for distribution, and removing it is a retreat rather than a fix. Their questions were the right ones: why can't the scanner add a serial, why can't the receipt form allow one, why not just add it.

THERE IS NO TECHNICAL REASON FOR EITHER GAP. Both screens already know the policy — the receipt form enforces one-unit-per-serial when a serial is typed, and the scanner recognises serial products in order to refuse them. Neither is missing information; both are missing input.

THREE PARTS. (1) The receipt form gains an add-line control, so ten serials means ten rows, PLUS bulk entry — typing 70 serials one row at a time is its own defect. (2) The scan console captures the serial at scan time, which is its natural home: the barcode IS the serial. (3) BOTH refuse the receipt when the policy says capture inbound and nothing was captured — that guard does not exist today and is the reason the gap is invisible. See also item 65's finding that receiving has no required field at all with a purchase order loaded.

Fix the scan console's message either way: it currently tells the truth about itself and a falsehood about the other screen.

_decisions.topic: Tax on purchase documents
_decisions.ruling: SHARED with sales. Tax rules are identical and driven by tax classes, so purchase documents reuse src/Contract/Tax/ (TaxCalculatorInterface, TaxContext, TaxLine) rather than growing a buy-side tax model. The flat typed tax field on AbstractPurchaseDocument is not the answer.

_decisions.topic: Fees on purchase documents
_decisions.ruling: NOT shared. Sales fees stay untouched. Purchase fees are new, separate logic with their own subscription seam, so bundles can register purchase fee calculators in future exactly as they can for sales today. Mirror the shape of the sales seam, not its code.

_decisions.topic: Purchase order completeness vs form sharing
_decisions.ruling: Completeness first. Build the buy side complete inside ProcurementBundle; consolidating with the sales form is a follow-up, if it is possible at all across the AbstractPurchaseDocument/AbstractSalesDocument boundary.

_decisions.topic: Units of measure — the model (SUPERSEDED 2026-09-11 by "Units of measure — NetSuite model")
_decisions.ruling: SUPERSEDED. Said quantity ratios must be per-product and weight/volume/length global. Replaced the same day after checking what NetSuite and Business Central actually do: NetSuite puts every ratio on the units type, including quantity, and gets per-product scoping from a per-item list of which units are available. See the next decision.

_decisions.topic: Units of measure — NetSuite model
_decisions.ruling: Follow NetSuite. One table, unit_of_measure, holds the terms AND the ratios for every family INCLUDING quantity — Box-12 and Box-24 are two distinct terms, each with its own ratio to the family base, exactly as NetSuite bakes the count into the unit ('assign Box a conversion rate of 8 and Pallet a conversion rate of 192'). Conversion is defined in exactly one place and nowhere else. Per-product scoping comes from a NEW join table listing which units are available on a given product, plus an OPTIONAL default unit — that is what stops the global vocabulary reaching the user, and it is the one enhancement over stock NetSuite. product_packaging_unit is retired: no per-product ratios anywhere. A product may declare NO units at all — some items do not participate, which is NetSuite's own behaviour (units are opt-in per item) and is the owner's ruling: blank is allowed.

_decisions.topic: Units of measure — one family per product
_decisions.ruling: A product belongs to ONE unit family — count, weight, volume or length — and the units available on it are drawn only from that family. NetSuite's shape exactly: the item names a units type, and its base, purchase, sale and stock units are all chosen from within it. A product is never both 'sold by weight' and 'sold by count' at the same time; a thing that genuinely is both is two products, or it is the case/unit SKU pair in item 22, which is a stock transaction and not a conversion.

_decisions.topic: Units of measure — a unit freezes once a document references it
_decisions.ruling: A unit_of_measure row cannot have its ratio changed once any document line points at it. Box-12 means twelve forever. Editing it to mean twenty-four would restate every invoice, order and estimate already written against it at once, with no movement recorded and nothing to reconcile — the same hazard per-product rungs were protected from, arriving on the global table because the table is now shared. A unit that needs a different ratio is a NEW unit (Box-24), and the product is repointed at it. ProductPackagingUnitService::assertUnreferenced() already implements exactly this refusal, naming each table.column and its row count, and discovers the columns from Doctrine metadata rather than a hand-kept list — it is ported to the global table, not deleted with the rest of packaging.

_decisions.topic: There is no production data
_decisions.ruling: Nothing is deployed and no real rows exist anywhere. So the never-write-to-existing-data caution does not apply to this app's own tables: product_packaging_unit and the fourteen packaging_unit_id / quantity_entered columns are DROPPED outright by #659, not orphaned, not backfilled, not kept readable for old documents. Any row presently in them is test or demo data and is expected to go with them. This is a fact about today and it expires the moment the first customer is live — the rule itself stands for everything after that, and the freeze-once-referenced ruling above is precisely what protects the data that does not exist yet.

_decisions.topic: AP aging — a bill with no due date
_decisions.ruling: Due IMMEDIATELY. A null vendor_bill.due_date is aged from the bill's own date, like any other bill — there is no separate 'no due date' column. It ages naturally: a ninety-day-old bill with no terms recorded lands in 90+, which is exactly where it belongs, because it is precisely the bill nobody is chasing. It is also the conservative assumption — assuming money is owed sooner never hides a liability, while 'we do not know' can. The screen must state the assumption, so a reader knows a bill may sit in 90+ because it carries no terms rather than because the vendor granted ninety days.

_decisions.topic: Unattended queue drain — merge policy
_decisions.ruling: Merge straight to main as work is verified, rather than staging on an integration branch. The owner chose this over the safer staging option after being told the trade-off: an unattended agent that merges a broken branch leaves main broken until something trips over it. The conditions that make it safe are therefore not optional — a branch is merged ONLY on a green suite run against the MERGED tree (never a branch-only green), and an item is marked done ONLY with a commit sha and the real suite numbers beside it.

_decisions.topic: Landed cost and cost accounting — parked
_decisions.ruling: PARKED, deliberately and with the consequence understood. Landed cost (freight, duty, brokerage allocated onto the unit cost of received goods) and the costing method behind it — FIFO or otherwise — are not being built now. Purchasing has too much broken at the level below: bills that can be paid twice, a vendor return that cannot be cancelled, a restock flag that moves no stock, screens that are sketches. The owner's framing: 'we have so many things to fix in purchasing, it is garbage work.' Right call — a correct landed cost sitting on top of a bill that can be double-paid is an accurate figure derived from a wrong one. Worth stating the cost of parking it so nobody rediscovers it as a surprise: until it exists, unit cost excludes freight and duty, so margin on imported goods reads high, and every price and margin report built on that cost inherits the error silently. Unpark it once the purchase documents themselves are trustworthy.

_decisions.topic: A green test suite is NOT evidence that a migration is correct
_decisions.ruling: Recorded as a standing fact about this repo, not a decision to revisit. tests/_bootstrap.php builds the Codeception schema by shelling out to `doctrine:schema:create --env=test`, from Doctrine METADATA — it explicitly does not replay migrations, and says so in its own comment ('schema:create does not run migrations'), which is why it has to seed the region reference rows by hand afterwards. So every full-suite green in this session, and every one before it, says nothing whatever about whether a migration applies, applies in the right order, or produces the schema the mapping expects. Migration correctness is proven by ONE thing: bin/ci-migration-replay. From now on every merge commit states which guarantee came from the suite and which from replay, and says the migrations are unproven when replay was not run rather than letting the suite's green imply otherwise. Any batch containing a migration gets a replay run reported as its own result beside the suite numbers.

_decisions.topic: Migration numbers are checked against the order branches LAND, not as a fresh chain
_decisions.ruling: Checking that a set of migration stamps sorts correctly is the wrong test. What matters is that no migration is numbered BELOW one that has already executed on a database. Concretely: main sat at Version20260911120000, the RFQ branch added 150000 and the bill branch 170000, which sorts perfectly as a fresh chain — but the bill branch lands first, so 170000 executes, and the RFQ's 150000 then arrives beneath it on every database already migrated. A fresh replay stays correct; every existing box runs it out of order. The rule: before a branch lands, renumber its migrations above whatever is already on main, and re-check at merge time rather than at write time. Renumbering is a rename and a class name, so it is always cheaper than reasoning about whether an out-of-order migration happens to be harmless. QUEUE.md records migration-number collisions biting this repo twice in one week; this is the same family of mistake wearing a different face.

_decisions.topic: Status is never hidden: big and loud on the detail page, a column in every list
_decisions.ruling: Owner ruling on item 41. The core rule at public/assets/css/app.css:611-615 that hides .lead and .eyebrow inside .panel-title-row is wrong and comes out. Status does not merely become visible again — it is displayed prominently on every document detail screen and as a column on every document list, on both the buy and the sell side. No screen may rely on prose or a page lead to disclose status. This is the display answer for item 40 as well: a voided bill reads Void.

_decisions.topic: Two branches landed in batch 7 that close no numbered item
_decisions.ruling: Recorded so the queue is not read as the whole history. feat/tracking-policy-screens (merge 80d33888) split tracking policies AND units of measure into separate list / new / edit screens, at the owner's direct instruction that 'in general save and list should be separate pages'; it was proven by measurement, the grid going from 44px — about the height of its own header row — to 737px inside an 852px clamp. feat/backorders-joins-the-grid-model (merge 13937ca3) brought backorders and carts into the grid model and introduced PLAIN_LISTS as a second register for non-grid lists. Correction to the record: I had told two mergers that KNOWN_OFFENDERS was already empty and that PLAIN_LISTS was its replacement ON MAIN. Both halves were false when they were told — at 5bfa1704 KNOWN_OFFENDERS still had four entries and PLAIN_LISTS did not exist on main at all, arriving only with this branch. Batch 6 then emptied KNOWN_OFFENDERS by conforming the screens, so the claim became true mid-flight for a reason I had not given. The two registers are also not replacements for one another: they police different rules.

_decisions.topic: Two operational facts from batch 5, one of them my own error
_decisions.ruling: (1) bin/test-slot's headroom is thinner than it looks. SUITE_PEAK_MB is 4000 and the observed Codeception peak has climbed 3.39 -> 3.47 -> 3.51 GB across three full runs in a single day as the suite grew. It is not a fixed property of the box; it tracks the test count, so it needs re-measuring whenever the suite grows substantially rather than being treated as settled. An under-estimate costs an OOM-killed run, which does not fail cleanly — it surfaces as bogus 'undefined method' errors that read exactly like real defects. (2) MY ERROR: I removed the worktree `batch5-mainbase` during a disk cleanup while batch 5 was actively using it as its PHPUnit baseline. My own filter was supposed to skip live agents' worktrees and I hand-listed `batch5-merge` while missing `batch5-mainbase` — the pattern, not the one name, is what needed skipping. Rule going forward: before removing any worktree, check it against EVERY live agent's whole prefix, not against a remembered list of directory names. An agent that mentioned this only in passing, buried under its result, had every right to lead with it.

_decisions.topic: Colour is a shared, core-owned trait vocabulary — no screen styles its own
_decisions.ruling: Owner ruling, given on item 42 and general in scope: "Colouring is fine but should use shared class names and core css defines all classes that we know of. So all objects with similar traits eg 'late' is same treatment." Three consequences. (1) Core CSS owns the vocabulary and defines every class it knows of; a screen or bundle does not invent one locally. (2) A trait is the same everywhere: 'late' renders identically on a purchase order, an invoice, a sales order and a backorder, because it is the same fact about the world, not a coincidence of appearance. (3) A bundle needing a trait core does not yet name asks for it to be ADDED to core. This also pre-settles the mechanism half of item 54 (status colour): the answer is a core trait vocabulary, not a hue per status slug, which is what let Accepted, Rejected and the rest silently render slate.

_decisions.topic: Every document prints and every document has a PDF, with the same buttons
_decisions.ruling: Owner ruling on item 44: "yes you need to do a full sweep. basically every doc has a pdf and print version. same button layouts." Print and PDF are a property of being a document in this app, not a feature some documents got. Identical button layout everywhere, so the control is learned once. Enforced by a conformance test that DISCOVERS documents and asserts both, never by a maintained list — which makes item 55 a prerequisite, since the existing discovery route is the CommercialDocument contract and GoodsReceipt, VendorReturn and Rfq are deliberately outside it.

_decisions.topic: A document stays editable until it is terminal; what has HAPPENED to it sets the floors
_decisions.ruling: Owner ruling on item 47, general in shape and borrowed from the sell side, which already had it right. A document locks for editing only in terminal states — Closed and Void on the sell side, Closed and Cancelled on the buy side. Everything in between stays editable, and what has already happened to a line sets the floor, one event per dimension: RECEIPTS floor quantity (a received line cannot be reduced below what arrived, nor deleted), BILLS floor price (a billed line's price is settled; a received-but-unbilled line is still correctable). Receiving and billing are different events and must not be collapsed into one 'touched' test. Where a bill's price disagrees with the order, that is a price-variance exception — already modelled in MatchLine and ThreeWayMatchService — not a refusal. Zoho, NetSuite and Dynamics all work this way; formal PO revisions are an enterprise add-on even in Dynamics and are NOT adopted.

_decisions.topic: A count tile renders only when it has something to report
_decisions.ruling: Adopted from NetSuite's Procurement Dashboard, which was looked up rather than recalled at the owner's instruction: reminders display ONLY when transactions matching their criteria exist, so a tile at zero is not rendered. This is the answer to 'don't fill a page for the sake of filling a page' — the page is short on a quiet day and long on a busy one, and every number on it is a thing somebody has to do. Applies to any counts-and-links screen this app grows, not only the procurement landing page. Also recorded: the owner ranked this work BELOW item 45, the bill-versus-invoice audit, in plain terms — worrying about dashboards while bills cannot add custom fees or lines the way the sell side can is the last thing to do.

_decisions.topic: Screen-polish decisions are delegated; core function comes first
_decisions.ruling: Owner ruling of 2026-09-12: "You can look them up with the worker and build it. Dashboard is not a priority when the core function isn't done - Not worth my time." Items 49, 50 and 51 — the exceptions screen's money column and row actions, the RFQ vendor checkbox wall, and bad parent ids on create screens — are decided by research and built, not brought back for a ruling. The standing order of work is core function first: item 45 and the reopened item 15, making the bill do what the invoice does. The test for interrupting the owner is whether a choice is irreversible or expensive, not whether it is a choice.

_decisions.topic: A ruling on one item is not a ruling on the ones near it
_decisions.ruling: My error, recorded because it cost the owner time to catch. They said the dashboard was not worth their time, which was a ruling on item 48; I read it as a general delegation and marked items 49, 50 and 51 decided without them. They corrected it: "Do it one by one. Don't skip 3 just cuz I made a statement." A statement about one item's priority says nothing about the items next to it in a list, and widening it is not efficiency — it silently removes decisions the owner intended to make. Item 49 they then approved outright; 50 and 51 are back to awaiting a ruling.

_decisions.topic: The front of the purchasing chain is parked; contract before tendering
_decisions.ruling: Owner ruling of 2026-09-12: requisition, purchase request, RFQ tendering, purchase contract and blanket order are ALL parked as future features and recorded on GitHub #662 — they add easily once the app is done and none of them blocks it. When they are built the order is PURCHASE CONTRACT FIRST, then RFQ tendering. That ordering is not arbitrary: an awarded RFQ produces a purchase contract, not a purchase order, so tendering has nowhere to land until contracts exist. The existing half-built RFQ is HIDDEN, not deleted — its entities, screens and tests stay for #662 to build on. Also recorded from the research behind this: purchase request and requisition are ALTERNATIVES rather than sequential steps, differing by whether the requester already knows the vendor; and no reference product ships both a tender RFQ and a purchase quote — NetSuite has only the RFQ, Business Central only the quote.

_decisions.topic: If there is an issue, be clear and be loud
_decisions.ruling: Owner ruling of 2026-09-12, generalised from item 51 in their own words: "general rule is if there's an issue be clear be loud." This is now the standing rule for every failure surface in the app, not only bad parent ids. Three things it forbids, all of which this codebase has done somewhere: failing SILENTLY (the Restock checkbox that moved no stock and said nothing; the search box wired to a handler nobody wrote); failing QUIETLY WRONG by guessing what the user probably meant (the lists that fell OPEN on an unresolvable customer id and showed every customer's documents; a date filter that also returns rows with no date); and failing OBSCURELY, where something is technically reported but nobody can act on it (a raw 400, or a 28KB string diff for a one-row difference). The positive form: say what is wrong, in the user's language, where they are looking, and loudly enough that it is not mistaken for success. Sits alongside the status ruling of item 41 — "status should be in tables and on the detail page, big and loud" — which is the same instinct applied to state rather than to errors.

_decisions.topic: Payments on both sides share one declared shape, not two parallel builds
_decisions.ruling: Owner ruling of 2026-09-12: "Payments in both sides should share a shape through our common strategy." An invoice payment and a vendor bill payment express the same idea — money recorded against a document — so they share a contract the way documents already share CommercialDocument, with a conformance test that DISCOVERS implementors rather than keeping a hand-written list, exactly as EveryDocumentDeclaresItsContractTest does. Shared: identity, amount, currency, date, method, reference, actor, the document it is against, and the move operation with its status recalculation on both documents. Per-side and DECLARED rather than hidden: how derived paid status is computed and by what, and anything customer-facing, which the buy side has no version of. A real asymmetry is never flattened to make the shape prettier — the precedent is VendorBillStatus, where claimsOrderedQuantity() includes drafts and counts() excludes them, each docblock naming the other. A shared shape makes differences visible; it does not hide them. Note the contract probably has to live in core, so the freeze applies and the boundary gets reported rather than crossed.

_decisions.topic: Technical Docs is tech support only
_decisions.ruling: Owner ruling of 2026-09-12: "tech support only. No one else can see." The admin sidebar's Technical Docs section — generated by TechnicalDocsBundle from a recursive Finder over docs/*.md — is gated to tech support and invisible to every other admin, ROUTE as well as menu row. This supersedes the question of whether to exclude a docs/ subtree: the mix of reference material and the repo's own working notes stops mattering once only support can see any of it. Consequence worth stating: the default sidebar fixture loses those rows, which also removes the trap where adding any markdown file under docs/ silently changed a byte-compared fixture.

_decisions.topic: An unresolved import lands as a Draft and is queued for escalation, not silently usable
_decisions.ruling: Owner ruling of 2026-09-12 on item 9. A product imported with a pack size where a unit was expected becomes a DRAFT and joins an escalation queue, rather than being flagged-but-usable or hard-blocked. The reference products all make the unit mandatory at creation, so none of them has this state at all: Zoho skips the row into a fix-and-reimport file, and Business Central makes the base unit unchangeable once a ledger entry has posted against the item. That last point is the argument: stock moving at an unknown unit is precisely the state in which the unit can no longer be corrected, so allowing it to transact turns a pending problem into a permanent one. Draft states the reason in vocabulary the app already speaks, needs no new column (ProductCore::$status exists), keeps the row visible and editable, and turns the backlog into a work list.

_decisions.topic: Targeted tests and fast pushes; one full suite at a checkpoint, not per worker
_decisions.ruling:
Owner ruling of 2026-09-12, and it is a correct diagnosis of a deadlock I had built. Twelve agents were each running the FULL suite against three memory slots, so every time main moved everyone re-queued and re-ran, and the queue never drained. Their words: "They are running full suite so every time it rebase everyone gets pushed back. Instead to verify fast, very specific cest only. Push fast asap. Get rid of workers. Have 1 worker do full cest after a major checkpoint. Otherwise a 1 line change will cost you 24 hours."

THE RULE. (1) A worker verifies with the specific Cests that could plausibly be affected by its own change, and nothing else. (2) It pushes as soon as those are green — it does not hold work back for a broad run. (3) Most targeted runs need NO memory slot: AdminMenuDefaultSidebarCest is 3 tests, 0.7s, 64MB, and bin/test-slot exists to stop concurrent FULL suites OOM-killing each other, not to gate small runs. (4) When main moves, a worker does NOT restart verification — it looks at what actually changed between its merge base and the new tip and re-runs only what that could touch; docs commits and cache-buster bumps touch nothing. (5) Every report and merge commit states WHAT WAS RUN and why it was sufficient. An argued targeted run beats an unfinished full one. (6) Completeness is covered at FLEET level: one worker runs the full suite as a checkpoint after a wave lands, not every worker before every push.

This does NOT relax any of the evidence rules. Conducted tests, positive controls, the row that must not change, proving a measurement rather than eyeballing it, and the migration statement all still apply — those are targeted tests by nature and are the cheap part. What is being cut is the reflex full-suite run, which was buying almost nothing and costing everything. The one exception: a change whose blast radius genuinely cannot be bounded — the product-status work touching ~20 readers including DQL and SQL filters is the live example — where the worker says so and asks for a slot rather than guessing.

_decisions.topic: ProductReceivingRule vs TrackingPolicy
_decisions.decision: ProductReceivingRule derives lot/serial/expiry from the product TrackingPolicy; the three duplicated columns are dropped. location_required stays its own column, per product — ruled final, no appeal. ADD-only migration rule overruled for this change only.
_decisions.why: Receiving already had all four guards. They never fired because ruleFor() returned an empty rule when no row existed, and nothing in the app ever created rows. The fix is redirecting the lookup, not building guards.

_decisions.topic: Fee rendering on sell-side documents
_decisions.decision: The ORDER detail screen is the authority for how fee lines render. main_line fees are rows in the line table body; before_tax_line sits in the totals box above the tax rows; after_tax_line sits below Total Tax. The invoice detail screen currently dumps all three into its tfoot and must conform.
_decisions.why: A fee placed after tax printed above the tax rows on the invoice screen, so the figures did not read as the arithmetic that produced the Total, and the invoice screen disagreed with its own PDF. A main-line fee is a line item by design and appeared in the footer instead.

_decisions.topic: Sell-side document template frame and customisation
_decisions.decision: Estimate, sales order and invoice share one base template plus shared components, on both the form and the detail side. The frame is ours and fixed; users add content within predefined slots. The skeleton renders from an ORDERED LIST of block slugs, hard-coded for now, so tenant-configurable order and visibility is a later swap of the list source rather than a template rewrite. Blocks carry a movable flag. The money section — line items, fees, shipping, tax, totals — is ANCHORED and cannot be reordered or switched off, because it is an arithmetic sequence. Header, info card, addresses, activity log, notes and terms are movable. Block slugs are stable identifiers and must not be renamed once tenants save layouts.
_decisions.why: Users will eventually customise these documents: templates, field visibility and labels, and their own custom fields, all yes; free-form layout no. Component boundaries are therefore customisation units, so cutting them for tidiness alone would mean re-cutting them later. Line items and the money rows are structural: a document whose tax sits above its fees stops explaining how it reached its own total.
_decisions.unique_blocks: Only these do not share: estimate TBD pricing, estimate accept-on-behalf, invoice Record Payment and its payments page, order batch/lot cell, plus per-document action-bar items. Everything else is shared, parameterised, or a gap to fill.

_decisions.topic: Two bases, one component set
_decisions.decision: The sell-side edit screens share one base template and the detail screens share another. They do NOT share a single skeleton. Both bases draw on ONE shared component set (address panel, line row, line table, totals, activity log, status field, action bar).
_decisions.why: A form posts and a view does not, so one skeleton serving both would branch on that everywhere. The components are the same either way, which is where the duplication actually lives.

_decisions.topic: Customisation is view-only
_decisions.decision: Tenant customisation — templates, field visibility, relabelling, custom fields — applies to the DETAIL/view screens only. The EDIT forms are fixed and set by us. The block-list skeleton and its stable slugs therefore belong to the view base alone; the edit base needs none of it.
_decisions.why: Amends the earlier frame decision, which did not separate the two. Building the edit forms for configuration that is never coming to them would be indirection with no caller.

_decisions.topic: An invoice custom field is write-once
_decisions.decision: Invoice custom fields are captured when the invoice is raised and are never editable or displayed afterwards. Accepted as the shipped behaviour; revisit only if somebody asks to edit one.
_decisions.why: There is no invoice edit screen in this application — admin_invoice_edit does not exist, confirmed in debug:router and stated outright in invoice/_tab_nav.html.twig and InvoiceController::create(). Custom fields render on forms only, and an invoice has no form after creation. May well be right for an accounting record, but it is a consequence somebody should hold deliberately rather than discover.

_decisions.topic: The relabel guard went blind when labels moved into column lists
_decisions.decision: AdminTemplatesCallTheBuyerACustomerTest must scan quoted values of human-facing keys (label, title, placeholder, data-label) INSIDE Twig tags. Everything else in a tag stays out of scope.
_decisions.why: Tonight's shared-partial refactors moved user-facing labels into {% set rows = [{label: 'Company Name', ...}] %}. The scanner strips {% %} by design, so those labels became invisible to it — and the pattern is spreading through every new partial. The three stale ALLOWED entries were the symptom; the blind spot is the defect.

_decisions.topic: A queue entry is a claim, not a fact — verify before building
_decisions.decision: Every worker brief must tell the agent to verify the entry's premise against main FIRST and report if it is already done, rather than rebuilding it.
_decisions.why: Three entries tonight (37, 52, 53) described defects already fixed on main, and one brief's stated premise — 'purchase_order_edit.html.twig still renders a province select' — was simply false. Workers that checked first found the genuinely-undone remainder instead: the three-way match warehouse comparison, and a literal @env in prose that was registering a bogus Codeception environment on every gate run. The wasted alternative was rebuilding what existed and missing what did not.

_decisions.topic: A conducted test must post what the PAGE renders, not a payload it builds
_decisions.decision: Cests that exercise a form must read off the rendered page everything a browser would submit and post that. FunctionalTester::grabFormPayload() does this; prefer it to hand-building a payload.
_decisions.why: The stock-override reason field was fully working server-side, covered by passing Cests, and rendered on NO screen for weeks — an over-stock save could only ever be refused in a browser. A hand-built payload posts fields no screen renders just as happily as fields it does, so the suite was green over a feature nobody could reach. This is the same blindness class as #627's bare see().

_decisions.topic: The test environment can lie, and did
_decisions.decision: Test bootstraps must empty the framework cache pool alongside the database wipe, not just sweep var/cache/test.
_decisions.why: Symfony 7.4 moved framework.cache to %kernel.share_dir% — var/share/<env>, deliberately OUTSIDE the cache dir so it survives cache:clear. AppSettings caches the whole settings table for an hour, so one test writing default_sales_tax_code='E' poisoned every later run from disk. The tell was a first run reporting 1 failure and every run after reporting 3. Two of those failures were then read as a tax money bug that did not exist.

_decisions.topic: Truncation is rarely only in the column
_decisions.decision: When a quantity column is the wrong type, fix the whole path: the column, every cast above it, and the figures any message derives from it.
_decisions.why: The four *_stock_override quantity columns were integer, but AdminOrderStockValidator did (int) round((float) qty) three layers higher — so 50.5 became 51, MORE than was asked for, and the shortfall sentence's three figures did not subtract. Widening the column alone would have left a correct column fed by a truncating system.
